title: Cultural Humility
subtitle: Learning what something means to the person, examining your own reading, and minding the influence your role carries
summary: Knowing a service well does not mean knowing what it means to every person who uses it. This course builds cultural humility as the readings define it: ongoing self-examination, attention to unequal influence, and partnership that gives people a real choice. You practice separating what someone said from the meaning you added, asking questions with a purpose, hearing a correction without defending yourself, and carrying what you learn into the structured tools and real responsibilities of DHS work. A workplace simulation lets you try these moves when a member of the public says a DHS appointment letter left her lost outside the building.
objectives: Explain cultural humility as an ongoing practice of self-examination, attention to unequal influence and partnership, and say what it is not.
Separate what a person actually said or did from the meaning your own learned experience added to it.
Ask a question with a clear purpose that lets the person's answer change your interpretation, without making personal disclosure the price of help.
Respond to a correction by naming the specific inference you got wrong, without defending your intention or asking for reassurance.
Use structured tools and real responsibilities alongside humility, and describe what you learned, what you did and what is still unknown as different things.

segments.title: Welcome and why it matters

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Cultural Humility. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, facing the viewer with a warm, open expression, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: Cultural Humility
Learning what something means to the person, and examining your own interpretation
scenes.narration: Welcome to Cultural Humility. You bring knowledge of programs, forms and working relationships to the decisions you make in your role at DHS. That knowledge becomes more useful when you can recognize what it does not tell you about another person's experience. A process that seems clear from inside a team may convey something quite different to someone using it for the first time. Cultural humility means examining that difference without dismissing either professional knowledge or the person's account of what happened. It asks you to consider your interpretation, remain open to correction, and recognize the influence that comes with your public-service role. Throughout this course, you will examine those duties through practical examples, questions for reflection and a workplace simulation. The purpose is to strengthen your judgment when an established explanation and another person's experience do not yet fit together.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Correct and still hard to use. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned slightly toward the points, one hand raised toward the second line.
on_screen: The address is correct.
The entrance is still hard to find.
Both accounts answer different questions.
scenes.narration: Consider an appointment letter that gives the correct building address but leaves a visitor unsure which entrance to use. Staff have verified the address, while the visitor describes walking around the building without finding a recognizable public door. These accounts concern different aspects of the same service: locating the building and successfully entering it for an appointment. Responding that the directions are complete treats the first question as though it also resolves the second. The visitor's experience then disappears from the team's assessment, even though it identifies a practical condition staff have not examined. This example does not establish anyone's intention or prove that every visitor encounters the same difficulty. It shows why professional accuracy needs to be considered alongside the conditions under which people actually use a service. When repeated concerns are dismissed as already resolved, arrangements can continue favoring people who possess knowledge that newcomers have never received.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two sides of humility. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, gesturing first toward one point, then toward the other.
on_screen: Inward: an accurate view of yourself, including your limits
Outward: focus on the other person, with curiosity
scenes.narration: Joshua Hook, Don Davis, Jesse Owen and Cirleen DeBlaere are counseling psychologists who describe two sides of humility in helping relationships. Looking inward means recognizing your own perspective and its limits, while looking outward means taking an interest in another person's experience. In the studies described in the reading, clients' ratings of their therapist's cultural humility predicted the working relationship and treatment outcomes. That finding gives a reason to examine how people experience professional help, but it does not guarantee that one conversation will improve an outcome. Most of the evidence comes from therapy and relies on clients' accounts, so its use in benefits or policy work needs care. The reading also raises a concern: focusing on personal humility can leave unequal conditions built into a service unexamined. In DHS work, consider your own assumptions alongside the rules, resources and power to make decisions that shape the person's experience.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: The path ahead. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, half-turned toward the list, one hand open toward it.
on_screen: What it is, and your own assumptions
Curiosity, listening and repair
Your work, then a workplace simulation
scenes.narration: The course begins with the meaning of cultural humility and the assumptions that shape how you read another person's behavior. It then examines curiosity, listening and respect, including how a well-intended question can pressure someone to share more than the task requires. The next section considers repair: noticing a mistaken inference, responding to a correction and addressing effects that have already reached other people. Finally, you will connect those practices with structured tools and the duties that apply to actual decisions at DHS. Questions at the end of each section offer a way to think through the reasoning privately or discuss an example with a trusted colleague. As you begin, consider a conversation, letter or meeting in which your understanding of the process differed from someone else's experience. Returning to that situation throughout the course can help you identify a specific question or response worth reconsidering.

check.prompt: A person says the appointment letter did not help them find the public entrance. Staff confirm the address is correct. Which reading fits the example best?

options.text: The address answers where the building is, and the person's account answers whether someone new can get in. Both belong in the response.

feedback.text: You kept both accounts in view. The checked address stays useful, and the person's experience points to something the letter does not yet say. Build on that by asking which part of the route was unclear.
Next time you hear a concern like this, try: “The address is right, so tell me where along the way it got confusing.”

options.text: Staff checked the address against the official listing and it is correct, so the letter is accurate and the concern can be closed with a polite reply.

feedback.text: The address check answers where the building is. The concern is about which door to use. A stronger response keeps the accurate fact and still asks about the gap the person found.
From outside the building, a correct address can still leave you walking past doors that all look alike. The person knows something staff cannot see from inside.

options.text: If one person could not find the door, many others likely could not either, so the whole letter should be rewritten before it goes to anyone else.

feedback.text: Wanting to fix it fully is a caring reaction. One account shows a real gap worth examining; it does not yet show what every visitor needs. Start with the specific difficulty.
What would you want to learn before deciding how big the change should be?

When has someone's account of your work told you something you could not have seen from your side?

segments.title: What cultural humility is and is not

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three commitments. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, standing upright and speaking to the viewer.
on_screen: Ongoing self-examination
Attention to unequal power
Respectful partnership
scenes.narration: Tervalon and Murray-García introduced cultural humility in a 1998 paper about medical education, with three commitments that continue throughout professional practice. Lifelong self-examination means considering how your own learned expectations shape what you notice and how you interpret another person's response. Attention to power means recognizing the imbalance between a professional who controls parts of a service and someone seeking assistance. Partnership means working with people in ways that benefit both parties, without assuming that professional authority settles what matters to them. The original setting involved doctors and patients; the DHS examples in this course draw on those concepts without borrowing clinical procedures. The same questions can inform how you explain a notice, answer a call, organize a meeting or review a proposed policy. They provide a basis for examining judgment and relationships, rather than a universal legal rule or procedure for every DHS program.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two friends and one offer. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse, with locs (C2) stands full length, relaxed, with a small friendly smile, as the second friend, who declined the offer.
on_screen: What happened: the second friend declined help packing.
What the first friend heard: distance.
What the second friend said: nothing about the friendship.
scenes.narration: One reading follows two friends preparing for a move, whose different understandings of practical help lead to a mistaken conclusion. The first friend learned that accepting help expresses trust and shared care; the second learned that making arrangements independently avoids imposing on others. When the second friend declines help with packing, the first interprets that decision as evidence that the friendship matters less. The refusal itself does not establish that meaning, and neither person's experience needs to be explained through nationality or group membership. The second friend can value the relationship while preferring to manage this particular task without assistance. A question such as “Would help feel useful, or would you rather make the arrangements yourself?” leaves both possibilities available. Cultural humility keeps the first interpretation open long enough for the other person's meaning to inform the next response.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What it is not. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, one hand raised slightly, counting the points off.
on_screen: Not just modesty
Not giving up your expertise
Not agreeing to everything or setting aside real duties
scenes.narration: Cultural humility involves more than admitting that your knowledge is limited or presenting yourself as a modest professional. It requires examining how your expectations affect an exchange and whether another person's account can change your understanding or response. Your expertise remains important: a community brief can supply useful history, and your role can provide information that someone needs. Neither source establishes everything about that person's circumstances, priorities or preferred way of proceeding with the task. Understanding a request also does not require agreeing to it; you can explain an actual limit while exploring an available alternative. Making a promise you cannot fulfill would leave the person with a less reliable basis for deciding what to do next. Humility strengthens the judgment behind your response while leaving formal decisions with the person or area responsible for them.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Knowledge and meaning. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the royal blue blouse (C5) stands full length, holding a worn serving bowl in both hands, as the bowl's owner.
on_screen: Knowledge: what the object was made for
The person's meaning: what it means to them now
scenes.narration: Cultural humility and cultural competence are sometimes presented as opposing approaches, but the readings offer a more careful distinction. Tervalon and Murray-García challenged competence understood as finished mastery, while Hook and his colleagues questioned the goal of mastering facts about groups. The National Center for Cultural Competence describes an ongoing process that includes self-assessment and adaptation alongside learning about other people. Those approaches can support one another when knowledge remains open to correction through the person's account of what matters. In one example, a person researches the age, materials and customary uses of an old bowl that a friend inherited. The researcher then assumes the bowl should remain untouched on a shelf, while its owner explains that careful daily use keeps a loved person present. Historical knowledge informs the conversation, but it cannot settle the meaning that the bowl now carries for its owner.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A stance, not a credential. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands at rest.
on_screen: A stance, not a credential
Knowledge informs the question. It does not answer for the person.
scenes.narration: The Hook reading describes cultural humility as a stance rather than a credential: a continuing approach to learning through relationships. Completing a course cannot establish that someone understands every culture, and labels such as humble or competent do not describe what actually occurred. A specific account is more useful because it identifies the interpretation that changed, the evidence behind that change and the response that followed. In the bowl example, the researcher retained useful historical knowledge while reconsidering an assumption about how the owner should use it. That is a meaningful change in understanding, even though it does not establish mastery or settle the next question. The same distinction applies when you describe learning from a conversation about a DHS service or a colleague's work. Knowledge can improve the question you ask, while the person remains the source of their own meaning and priorities.

check.prompt: Which description of cultural humility matches the readings?

options.text: An ongoing practice: examining your own interpretations, noticing unequal influence and working in partnership, while still using what you know.

feedback.text: You held all three ideas together and kept knowledge in the picture. Extend it by noticing which of the three you lean on least in your own work.

options.text: Being honest that you cannot know everything about other cultures, and saying so openly, so people know you are not claiming to be an expert on their lives.

feedback.text: Admitting limits is a start. The readings ask for more: examining how your expectations shape the exchange, and letting the other person's account actually change your response.

options.text: Building solid knowledge of each cultural group's customs and values, so you can anticipate what the people you serve will want before they have to explain.

feedback.text: Learning facts about groups can feel like useful preparation. Those facts can help you frame a question, but they cannot establish one person's priorities. Leave room for the person to explain what matters in this situation.

options.text: Setting your own expertise aside so the person's view leads, and agreeing to what people ask, because they know their own lives best.

feedback.text: A person relying on you needs your knowledge and honest limits. Agreeing to everything can leave them with promises no one can keep.

reflection: Which of the three commitments, self-examination, attention to power or partnership, comes most easily to you? Which takes more effort?
Think of something you know well about a community or a program. What question about one person does that knowledge still leave open?
Where have you seen humility mistaken for agreeing to everything?

segments.title: Looking at your own assumptions

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Observation or added reason. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned slightly toward the two sentences, one hand open.
on_screen: Observation: “The form was not returned.”
Added reason: “The person is not interested.”
scenes.narration: Compare the statement “The form was not returned” with the conclusion “The person is not interested.” The first describes an observable event; the second supplies a reason that the event alone cannot establish. A missing form could reflect unclear instructions, a practical barrier, disagreement, changed plans or circumstances the staff member has not encountered. Each explanation would support a different response, which is why distinguishing the event from its possible causes matters for the work. Sound judgment separates what is known, what might explain it and what additional information could clarify the next step. This does not require treating every explanation as equally likely or doubting facts that have already been checked. It requires noticing when your account moves beyond the evidence and asking whether the person supplied that meaning or you did.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What was asked, what was added. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4) stands full length, holding a printed sheet with two appointment options, as the staff member at the counter.
on_screen: The person asked: to compare options with someone she trusts.
The staff member added: she is reluctant to decide.
scenes.narration: In a DHS appointment practice example adapted from the readings, a staff member has prepared a clear explanation of two appointment options. The person listening asks, “Can I compare the arrangements with someone I trust before I choose?” Because the staff member believes his explanation is complete, he interprets this question as reluctance to make a decision. She has asked about seeking advice, however, and has not supplied the motive he assigns to that request. If he treats reluctance as established, his next response may pressure her to choose before her practical question is answered. Keeping her actual words in view instead gives him a reason to ask what she wants to compare. He can then explain the arrangements that the appointment process allows, without confusing his preparation with knowledge of her priorities. The difference lies in the interpretation guiding his response, rather than in the information that she originally provided.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Learned meanings. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, speaking to the viewer, hands loosely together.
on_screen: A settled answer can show respect for someone's time.
A shared question can show respect for a shared result.
Neither is a rule for a group.
scenes.narration: The example then explores why the staff member's interpretation initially feels reasonable to him, rather than treating it as inexplicable prejudice. He remembers a school debate group where preparing a complete position before inviting questions expressed respect for the audience. A colleague describes learning a different approach in a community orchestra, where shared questions helped people decide how to play a passage. Both accounts connect preparation with responsibility, but they give different meanings to a question raised before a decision is complete. The person seeking the appointment then explains, “I want to ask my friend about travel time. I still want to tell you which route I choose.” Her explanation shows how consulting someone can support her own decision rather than signal a refusal to make it. These meanings belong to the people describing their experiences; they do not establish expectations for a nationality, family or every musician.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three paths after a reaction. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, standing calmly, speaking gently to the viewer.
on_screen: Self-blame: “My value is a flaw.”
Self-defense: “My value is right, so they should accept it.”
Self-examination: “Does my value fit this moment?”
scenes.narration: Examining an assumption does not require rejecting the value that made it feel reasonable in the first place. In the friendship example, the first friend remembers neighbors sharing tasks during a difficult period, when accepting help expressed belonging. That experience helps explain the reaction to a refused offer, but it does not determine what the second friend owes. Self-blame would dismiss the value as foolish and replace one rigid conclusion with another, without learning what the refusal meant. Self-defense would list reasons why help is worthwhile and conclude that the other person should accept it. Self-examination instead asks whether the connection between help and belonging explains this particular refusal, given what the friend actually said. The first friend can continue valuing mutual support while changing how it is offered and respecting the other person's decision. The practice concerns your reasoning; it does not depend on shame or sharing a personal history.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A request, not a reason. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned toward the points, one hand lightly raised.
on_screen: Valuing family is not the same as wanting family in every conversation.
Ask what participation means now.
scenes.narration: Good intentions can also conceal assumptions about what another person should find helpful in a particular situation. In one reading, staff invite family members to a planning conversation because they understand family involvement as a source of support. When the person asks to speak privately, that request identifies the arrangement they want without necessarily explaining the reason. Staff do not need to fill the gap with a cultural explanation or require a personal history before considering the request. Someone can value family relationships while wanting to discuss a particular issue alone, and preferences can change with the circumstances. The useful questions concern the purpose of this conversation, the support the person chooses and the arrangements available for meeting that need. Allowing the answer to inform the response keeps a general value from becoming a fixed instruction imposed on an individual.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Narrow the label. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, holding a small notepad and pen.
on_screen: “Quiet in the meeting” is narrower than “not committed.”
“Questioned the instruction” is narrower than “does not understand the service.”
scenes.narration: A practical way to examine interpretation is to compare a familiar label with the narrower observation behind it. The readings offer examples such as declining help, remaining quiet during a meeting and questioning an instruction. None of those observations establishes that someone lacks commitment, rejects support in general or misunderstands the service being discussed. Start by describing what occurred, then identify an assumption you could reconsider and a question that might change your understanding. Consider where the broader label could travel if it remained unexamined, including a note, a meeting summary or a later decision. Describing someone as unwilling may influence the choices another staff member offers, even when the original exchange concerned only one arrangement. This brief check before writing or responding helps preserve room for evidence that does not fit your first account.

check.prompt: A staff member has prepared two appointment options. The person he is serving asks to compare them with someone she trusts, and he hears reluctance. What should he examine first?

options.text: The difference between what she actually asked for, a chance to compare the options with someone she trusts, and the reluctance he added to it.

feedback.text: You put the actual request back at the center. From there he can ask what she wants to compare and explain what the process allows. Try spotting the same gap in your own next exchange.
When did you last hear a question as hesitation, and what did the person actually ask?

options.text: Which cultural or family background might explain her hesitation, so he can respond in a way that fits what people like her usually expect.

feedback.text: A group explanation predicts her meaning without her. Examining his own inference lets him respond to what she actually said.
She asked a practical question. Being explained by a group label could leave her feeling unheard as a person.

options.text: Whether his explanation of the two options was clear and complete enough, since a gap in what he said could be why she wants a second opinion.

feedback.text: Good preparation can make an answer feel complete. Being prepared is valuable. It still cannot tell him which question remains open for her.
After explaining, try asking, “Which part would you like to look at more closely?”

reflection: Pick one label you used about someone at work this month. What did you actually observe?
What is a value you learned early that makes certain behavior feel respectful to you? Where might it not fit someone else?
Where could a first impression of yours travel after the conversation ends, such as a note, an assignment or a record?

segments.title: Curiosity, listening and respect in practice

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A question with a purpose. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, turned toward the two questions, one hand open toward the second.
on_screen: “Why are people from your community reluctant?”
“What part is difficult to use?”
scenes.narration: Curiosity supports cultural humility when the question serves a clear purpose and leaves the person's account open. Compare “Why are people from your community reluctant?” with “What part is difficult to use?” The first question supplies both a group explanation and a judgment about reluctance before the person has described the difficulty. The second identifies the task and invites information that could help staff respond to the actual concern. A question about someone's cultural history may interest the professional while adding little to the decision or assistance the person needs. Before asking, consider how the answer could change your interpretation, the options you explain or the next step you offer. If that connection is unclear, the question may be serving your curiosity more than the purpose of the exchange.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Help without a story. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the white blouse, with curly hair (C3) stands full length, at ease, holding a printed sheet of travel times, as the person being served.
on_screen: A person can decline to share and still get practical help.
No one represents a whole community.
scenes.narration: Curiosity can become a burden when staff ask someone to explain personal meaning before answering a practical question. In the appointment example, the staff member asks about the family tradition behind the person's wish to seek advice. She replies, “I would rather just compare the travel arrangements,” which identifies the assistance she wants at that moment. Her response does not establish distrust or a refusal of help, and it does not require an explanation about her background. Returning to travel times and the arrangements the process allows respects both the task and her control over what she shares. If she later offers more context, the staff member can listen without treating her experience as a statement about an entire community. Practical help must not depend on a personal story, and one person's account cannot establish what everyone with a similar background wants.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A brief prepares your questions. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a printed brief at his side.
on_screen: A brief prepares your questions.
It does not predict a person's answers.
scenes.narration: Community briefs can introduce history, language and experiences with institutions that a staff member might otherwise overlook. Their value depends on how that information enters the conversation, especially when a general pattern seems to explain an individual's request. One reading identifies claims about “how Hmong families are” as an example of turning background knowledge into a stereotype. Learning that some families value involvement in planning does not establish whom this person wants present or what they wish to share. Use the background to frame questions, then listen for the details that fit, differ or remain unknown in this situation. The bowl example shows the same problem when the researcher considers asking why its owner is not following the proper custom. That wording already treats a pattern as a rule; asking what daily use means to the owner leaves the explanation open.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Cultural opportunities. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, leaning forward slightly toward the viewer.
on_screen: Cultural opportunities: moments when identity comes to the front
No single identity explains a person.
scenes.narration: Hook and his colleagues describe cultural opportunities as moments when a person's identity or background becomes relevant within a conversation. Their framework treats noticing and responding to those openings as a professional skill that develops through practice and reflection. The reading also connects anxiety with reduced curiosity, suggesting that comfort with the discussion can affect how a professional responds. This is a reason to build experience thoughtfully, rather than to assume that more information about a group will resolve every difficulty. The authors emphasize that no single identity explains a person, whose experience may involve language, age, faith, disability and other circumstances together. When an opening arises, ask a relevant question that the person can decline without losing the practical assistance they sought. Their account can clarify this encounter, while leaving them in control of which aspects of their experience enter the conversation.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Being heard is not the same as influence. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, one hand on each side, as if weighing two things.
on_screen: Being heard is not the same as having influence.
Say what is decided, what is open and what the input can change.
scenes.narration: Listening to a concern and allowing it to influence a decision are related practices, but they are not interchangeable. In the friendship example, the person providing the vehicle proposes an early departure that would interrupt an important goodbye. Saying “I understand” without examining the timing acknowledges the concern while leaving the original plan entirely unchanged. There may be a real constraint, such as returning the vehicle that afternoon, alongside a departure time that could still be adjusted. Humility involves explaining that distinction and considering available choices, without promising an arrangement that cannot work. A supervisor encounters a similar issue when requesting ideas after announcing an assignment whose remaining choices have not been explained. Clarifying what is decided, what remains open and how a concern could affect the next step gives the invitation a credible purpose.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Carrying a question forward. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4) stands full length, holding a short printed summary, as the staff member who wrote it.
on_screen: Before: “The person has not made a decision.”
After: “The person wants to compare travel times with someone she trusts before choosing.”
scenes.narration: A public-service role often carries influence over the questions asked, the order of an explanation and the words another staff member receives. In the DHS appointment example, the worker's first summary states, “The person has not made a decision,” without including the question she raised. Although the statement is accurate, its emphasis could lead the next reader to send reminders rather than address the travel comparison. A fuller account explains that she wants to compare travel conditions with someone she trusts before choosing, and that the allowed arrangements need checking. That revision preserves her stated purpose while distinguishing it from the staff member's earlier assumption about reluctance. Cultural humility does not ask the worker to abandon responsibility for keeping an accurate record or explaining the service. It asks the worker to examine whether the account carries the person's meaning forward or quietly substitutes an interpretation of their own.

check.prompt: The person at the counter declines to talk about the family tradition behind her request and says she would rather just compare the travel arrangements. What should the staff member do?

options.text: Go back to the travel comparison, ask only questions that help with it, and leave room for her to share more later if she chooses.

feedback.text: You let her answer steer the conversation without treating it as a closed door. That keeps help available and leaves room for her to share more later if she chooses.
A line that works here: “Sure. Which travel times would be most helpful to look at together?”

options.text: Hold off on the options for now and gently ask once more about the tradition, since knowing her background would help him tailor them.

feedback.text: Pausing turns personal sharing into a condition for help. Returning to her actual question keeps both the help and her choice intact.
To her, it could feel like she has to explain her family before getting a straight answer about appointment times.

options.text: Add a note to her file that she seems wary of staff, so whoever helps her next is prepared and does not push the same questions.

feedback.text: A declined question can sting, and it is natural to look for a reason. Her reply did not supply distrust. Writing it down would carry an added meaning into the next conversation.
What did she actually say, word for word, and what would an accurate note contain?

reflection: Think of a question you often ask people you serve or work with. What do you do with the answer?
When did someone in a meeting ask for input on something already decided? How did it feel to be on the receiving end?
Where do you control the words in a record or summary that someone else will act on?

segments.title: When it goes wrong and how to recover

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Missed moments will happen. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, relaxed, with a small rueful smile.
on_screen: Missed opportunities will happen.
Repair without defensiveness is a core skill.
scenes.narration: The Hook reading treats missed cultural opportunities and microaggressions as problems that professionals need to recognize and repair without defensiveness. Preparing carefully matters, but it does not remove the possibility that your interpretation will miss something important to another person. The reading also questions the reliability of judging your own humility, because the same assumptions can shape both your response and your assessment of it. Feedback from people receiving a service, colleagues and supervisors can reveal effects that were not visible from your position. The purpose is to understand a particular exchange and improve the response, rather than to secure a favorable judgment about your character. Recovery therefore involves noticing the correction, examining what it changes and following through where your earlier account has affected the work.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A correction is information. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse, with locs (C2) stands full length, speaking openly, one hand raised, as the second friend explaining the refusal.
on_screen: A correction is information.
“I heard the refusal as distance, and I understand that was not what you meant.”
scenes.narration: A correction supplies information that your first interpretation did not include, whether it concerns a workplace request or a personal exchange. In the friendship story, the second friend explains, “I appreciated the offer. I wanted to manage the packing because accepting help would make me worry about owing you time you may need.” That account directly challenges the first friend's conclusion that declining help meant placing less value on the relationship. Responding “I heard the refusal as distance, and I understand that was not what you meant” identifies the inference being reconsidered. It does not ask the friend to defend a whole identity or provide reassurance about the other person's intentions. A further offer of help can remain available, with the second friend still free to decline it. The repair concerns this person's meaning in this situation, rather than a general explanation of how a group behaves.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three sideways repairs. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned toward the points, counting them off on one hand.
on_screen: Defending your intention
Asking for reassurance
Declaring it fixed
scenes.narration: Three responses can divert a repair away from the concern that prompted it, even when the intention is sincere. Explaining at length that you meant well keeps attention on your motives instead of addressing the interpretation or action that caused difficulty. Asking the other person to confirm that you are still caring or fair adds another demand to the exchange. Declaring the matter resolved after an apology confuses an action you have taken with an effect you have not yet established. The person may need time, a practical change or a correction elsewhere before they can judge what the apology means. A more useful response identifies what you misunderstood, checks whether the revised understanding is accurate and changes what falls within your responsibility. Leave room for the other person's account of the outcome, rather than treating your own sense of relief as evidence that the repair succeeded.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Where the first reading went. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, one hand raised, tracing a path in the air.
on_screen: Where did the first interpretation go?
A private change of mind may not reach a record or routine.
scenes.narration: Repair becomes more complicated when an interpretation has already reached a record or influenced how other people respond. One reading describes a note that presents someone as unwilling to involve others, although the person requested only one private conversation. A later reader could rely on that broader label when deciding which support or choices to offer in another situation. A similar problem arises when written comments from a newcomer are described as lack of commitment and then influence assignments. After recognizing the mistaken interpretation, consider where it traveled: a service note, a team summary, a planning discussion or someone's account of a meeting. Changing your own view privately will not correct information that other people continue to use in their decisions. Address the specific mistake through the responsibility you hold, while respecting privacy and avoiding a new explanation the person has not supplied.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A misunderstanding or a formal concern. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, upright and steady, speaking directly to the viewer.
on_screen: A misunderstanding and a formal allegation are not the same.
Supervisors and managers report protected-class allegations to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer immediately.
scenes.narration: An ordinary misunderstanding and an allegation requiring a formal response call for different actions, even when both arise during a difficult conversation. Reflection or a private apology cannot substitute for the required response to alleged harassment or discrimination based on a protected characteristic. Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report those allegations or incidents immediately to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. They also follow agency procedures, rather than waiting for proof, a group discussion or the end of a learning session. The readings identify similar boundaries when a concern involves a right, a complaint, a labor process, a safety duty or Tribal consultation. Contact the person or area responsible and follow the process that applies to the actual concern. Cultural humility can inform the respect shown throughout that response, but it cannot postpone or replace the duty itself.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Build comfort step by step. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, relaxed, with an encouraging expression.
on_screen: Avoiding the subject leaves the old default in place.
Comfort grows with practice.
scenes.narration: After a difficult exchange, withdrawing can feel safer than risking another question that might be received poorly. In the friendship story, the first friend considers avoiding the subject entirely, which would leave the interpretation of rejection unexamined. The absence of another disagreement would not show that the original misunderstanding had been resolved or that the relationship had improved. The Hook reading connects anxiety with reduced curiosity, providing a reason to build comfort through manageable practice and reflection. That does not require forcing yourself or another person into a demanding discussion before there is a useful purpose for it. A relevant question, with room to decline, can provide a smaller opportunity to listen and reconsider an interpretation. Notice what the exchange clarifies and what remains uncertain, so the next attempt draws on learning rather than a promise that practice always feels easier.

check.prompt: A colleague tells you, “That is not why I asked for the meeting to be moved.” You had told the team it was about avoiding a tough topic. What is the strongest next move?

options.text: Name the specific assumption you made, ask whether you now understand it correctly, and correct what you told the team.

feedback.text: You named the inference, checked your new understanding and corrected the account where it had been shared. Continue by checking whether another record or recipient also needs the correction.
Words that fit: “I assumed it was about the topic, and I was wrong. I will let the team know that was my guess, not your reason.”

options.text: Explain that you were only trying to help the team understand the change, so your colleague knows you meant well and were not criticizing them.

feedback.text: Your intention may well have been good. Opening with it, though, keeps the focus on you. Naming the assumption first addresses what your colleague actually raised.
Your colleague has identified an inaccurate explanation shared with the team. Address that account and ask about any remaining concern rather than assuming which part matters most to them.

options.text: Apologize warmly and sincerely, thank your colleague for telling you, and let the matter rest so it does not become a bigger deal for them.

feedback.text: Wanting a clean ending after an awkward moment is very human. An apology is a good start. The team still holds the wrong reason unless you correct it.
Where did your first explanation go, and who still believes it?

reflection: When someone last corrected your reading of them, what did you do in the first ten seconds?
Which of the three sideways repairs, defending, seeking reassurance or declaring it fixed, do you fall into most?
Who could give you honest feedback about how you work across differences, and what would make it easy for them?

segments.title: Bringing it into your work

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A fact sheet is not a person. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a printed analysis form at his side.
on_screen: A fact sheet is not a person.
A blank analysis is not humility.
scenes.narration: One reading describes a worker who rejects the Equity Analysis Toolkit on the grounds that humility cannot be captured in a form. The example distinguishes two responsibilities that need to operate together, rather than choosing between a structured process and a responsive conversation. Learning about a community cannot establish an individual's priorities, so staff still need to consider the person's account of what matters. Structured analysis serves a different purpose by making the basis for a decision visible, including whose experience informed it and which benefits and burdens were considered. Completing every field does not show that an important perspective was heard, while a thoughtful conversation does not establish that anyone followed through. Use the analysis process that applies to the decision and examine what the people affected say the available information misses. A fact sheet cannot speak for a person, and leaving an analysis blank does not demonstrate humility.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Arrangement or access. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a clipboard with a checklist.
on_screen: A contract is an arrangement.
Access is what people can actually use.
scenes.narration: A checklist can support professional judgment when the evidence behind each answer receives attention, rather than only the completed box. In a practice case, a service team marks interpreter services as available because it has a contract in place. The contract establishes an arrangement, but the team has not examined how people learn about the service or how requests are handled. It also has not checked what happens when an interpreter cannot be provided at the time the person needs one. Those unanswered questions concern usable access, which the existence of a contract alone cannot demonstrate. A stronger review retains the contract information, identifies the missing evidence and asks the people responsible how those conditions are checked. Organizational self-assessments from the National Center for Cultural Competence serve a similar purpose: examining service conditions rather than rating an individual employee.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Partnership with honest limits. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt, hair tied back (C7) stands full length, pointing to one line on a printed draft instruction, as the community member.
on_screen: Explain what input can change.
Do not hand staff work to the person who spoke up.
No one speaks for everyone.
scenes.narration: In one example, a community member explains that a proposed instruction gives an accurate route without showing how to recognize the public entrance. The person also describes a service that feels difficult to reach without insider knowledge, adding meaning to the practical concern. A useful response considers both accounts, explains what staff can change and offers the person a chance to review a revision. That invitation does not make the community member responsible for rewriting every letter or representing everyone who uses the service. It also does not turn their contribution into endorsement of a draft that remains unchanged after they raised a concern. When staff retain the decision, explaining that authority and the limits of the invitation gives the person a clearer basis for taking part. Repeatedly collecting accounts without considering them can consume people's time while leaving the condition they identified untouched.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Openness needs capacity. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a sheet of discussion questions.
on_screen: A welcome is a statement.
A usable route takes time, information and a way to respond.
scenes.narration: An invitation to contribute needs practical support if it is to provide a usable way into the work. In a practice orientation, a coordinator encourages questions and interprets quick public responses as a sign that participants are engaged. One participant explains that raising an unfinished question can feel like challenging the facilitator before understanding the purpose of the discussion. Time to consider the material first would make it easier to prepare a useful contribution, without changing the participant's interest in the topic. The coordinator can respond to that account without treating it as evidence about a group or the participant's identity. Sharing the discussion questions beforehand and explaining how to respond may help, provided the material arrives early enough to be useful. The same question applies during hiring, onboarding and supervision: what time, information and follow-through are needed to make an invitation workable?

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A request needs no special words. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the sage shirt and glasses (C1) stands full length, holding a short written note, as the employee asking for written information.
on_screen: A request does not need special words.
Forward it promptly, and tell the person who asked who will decide.
scenes.narration: In a practice example, an employee explains that hearing loss makes spoken briefings difficult and asks a supervisor for written information. The request identifies a disability-related work barrier without using the phrase reasonable accommodation, which Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1433 does not require. The person receiving the request forwards it promptly to the appropriate decision maker and tells the employee who that person is. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation; an appropriate request for that information belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator. Here, ADA refers to the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the coordinator's role belongs to the employment accommodation process. A learning discussion must not require the employee to explain a diagnosis or ask the team to vote on the request. Respect the employee's account while following the actual process, so reflection supports the response without replacing or delaying it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Learned, did, still unknown. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, turned toward the three points, one hand open.
on_screen: Confirm the concern. Name who can act. Say how people will hear back.
Insight, action and effect are different claims.
scenes.narration: Follow-through begins by confirming the concern, identifying who can respond and explaining how the person will hear what happens next. A date for returning to the question helps prevent a recorded conversation from becoming the final action while the barrier remains. When describing a change, distinguish what you learned, what you did and what evidence shows about its effect. Understanding a person's meaning is learning; revising a letter is an action; finding out whether the revision helps requires another source of evidence. Silence after the change does not prove that the difficulty disappeared, and one expression of thanks cannot establish that it works for everyone. The Hook reading asks how teams could develop feedback that helps staff understand people's actual experience of the service. Keeping unanswered questions visible allows a team to recognize progress without claiming effects that have not yet been examined.

check.prompt: A service review marks interpreter services as available because a contract exists. No one has checked how people learn about it or what happens when no interpreter is free. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep the contract fact, list the open access questions, and ask the people responsible for the service how those conditions are checked.

feedback.text: You kept what is known and made the gap visible. Next, add a date to come back to the answer so the question does not quietly close.
Try framing it as: “The contract is in place. What do people experience when they ask for an interpreter, and how would anyone know?”

options.text: Treat the contract as enough evidence for this review, since it commits the provider to the service, and note access as a topic for next year.

feedback.text: The contract shows an arrangement exists. The stronger response asks whether people can actually use it, which is the question the checklist was pointing at.
For someone waiting at a counter without the words they need, a contract on file does not help unless the request works in that moment.

options.text: Stop using the checklist for this item, since a checked box cannot prove access, and replace it with an open discussion at the next team meeting.

feedback.text: The checklist has identified an unanswered access question. Keep a clear record of the evidence needed, responsible staff and follow-up, whether the team retains this tool or adopts a better way to track the work.
Which checklist in your own work has a box that deserves a closer look?

reflection: Which structured tool in your work could do more if you asked the people affected what it misses?
Where have you seen people asked for input with no word afterward about what happened to it?
Pick one recent change you made. What did you learn, what did you do, and what do you still not know about its effect?

simulations.intro: Whatever your role at DHS, you may encounter information that seems accurate from inside the organization but is difficult for someone else to use. I want you to examine that gap as a peer whose influence comes from what you notice, ask and follow through on. In this scenario, a visitor’s account prompts you to review an appointment letter and distinguish a verified address from directions that help someone find the entrance.
simulations.title: The visitor letter
simulations.learner_role: You are a member of a small DHS team that keeps the appointment letter and web page up to date for people coming in person to a DHS building. You are a peer on the team, not its lead. Your teammates are an experienced teammate who has written the letter for years, a newer teammate who joined two months ago, and the team lead.
simulations.background: On Monday, a visitor emails the DHS team responsible for the appointment letter after struggling to identify the public entrance. She writes: “Your letter gave me the address, and I found the building. Then I walked around it twice. There were four doors and none of them said which one was for visitors. I almost went home and missed my appointment.” The team lead adds the concern to Tuesday's meeting agenda, where about twenty minutes are available to discuss the issue. The letter has been unchanged for three years, although the experienced teammate checked its address against the official listing last spring. You have a shared draft and a team tracker for recording decisions, responsibilities and the work that remains open.

decisions.setup: The team lead reads the visitor's email aloud before inviting colleagues to consider what the team should do about it. The experienced teammate speaks first: “The address is correct. I checked it myself. The directions are complete. People just need to read the letter.” The newer teammate continues taking notes without offering a view, leaving their interpretation of the email unknown to the group. The team lead looks around the table and asks, “Thoughts?” As colleagues turn toward you, consider which part of the visitor's account the checked address actually resolves.
decisions.prompt: What do you say about the visitor's email?

choices.text: “The address was checked, so the letter is accurate. Let's send her a warm thank-you, confirm the address, and invite her to call if she gets lost again.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate agrees and offers to reply, while the team lead accepts the suggestion after a brief hesitation. The newer teammate starts to speak, then returns to the notes as the tracker item is marked complete within two minutes. Later that afternoon, the experienced teammate shares a proposed response in the team chat: “Thank you for your feedback. We have confirmed the address in our letter is correct. If you need help finding us, please call.” The response has not been sent, leaving an opportunity to reconsider whether it addresses the entrance problem the visitor actually described.

feedback.text: Confirming the address answers where the building is. The visitor was telling the team which door to use is unclear. A stronger move keeps the checked address and asks her where the route broke down.

Wanting to close an item that looks already solved is a very normal meeting instinct, especially when a trusted colleague has checked the facts. The catch is that accurate and usable are different questions.
If you were the one circling the building, what would that thank-you reply tell you?

choices.text: “The address is right, but her point is which door is the public one. Could someone ask her where it got confusing, and could two of us walk the route?”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate pauses before acknowledging the distinction: “Fair. The address and the door are two different things.” The team lead offers to ask the visitor which part of the route was unclear, keeping her account relevant to the review. The newer teammate then explains that the letter specifies the north entrance even though no outside sign identifies north. That detail is new to the experienced teammate, whose earlier check focused on the accuracy of the building address. The team lead records two next steps, asking the visitor and walking the route, so the meeting continues with a defined question still open.

feedback.text: You kept your teammate's checked fact and the visitor's experience side by side, and you turned the concern into two concrete next steps. Notice that your question gave the newer teammate an opening too. Keep looking for who else in the room has knowledge the discussion has not reached yet.
For the visitor, a reply asking where it got confusing says her walk around the building counted for something. That is very different from being told the address is correct.
When you walk the route, go in as someone who has never been there. Try to find the visitor door using only the letter, then note the exact point where you have to guess.

choices.text: “If she got lost, others probably did too. Let's rewrite the letter from scratch and redo the web page this week, so we fix every gap at once.”
choices.consequence: The team lead welcomes the willingness to act but hesitates over the scale of the proposed work and its deadline. The experienced teammate crosses his arms and asks, “One email and the whole letter is broken?” Discussion shifts toward workload and responsibility for rewriting, while the visitor's account receives no further examination and the newer teammate remains quiet. The team lead asks everyone to comment on the current letter by Friday, when she will decide the scope of any revision. The entrance question remains unresolved beneath a broader disagreement about work that the team has not yet established is necessary.

feedback.text: Taking a concern seriously enough to want a full fix is a caring reaction. One account shows a real gap; it does not yet show what every visitor needs or that everything else is wrong.

A stronger move starts with the specific difficulty the visitor named, which door, and finds out more before sizing the change. That also keeps the experienced teammate's knowledge of the letter in the conversation.
To the experienced teammate, “rewrite it from scratch” can sound like years of careful work dismissed. He may defend the letter instead of looking at the door problem.

choices.text: “Before we change anything, do we know anything about her? Maybe she's new to the area, or English isn't her first language. That would tell us who we should write for.”
choices.consequence: After a brief silence, the experienced teammate says, “Could be. Most people find it fine.” The team lead notes that the email provides no information about the visitor's background, while the newer teammate frowns without joining the discussion. Even so, the conversation continues to focus on possible explanations about the person rather than the four doors she described. The experienced teammate offers to send a polite confirmation of the address, and the item ends without examining the entrance problem. The team's proposed response now depends on an assumption that the visitor neither offered nor needed to explain her concern.

feedback.text: Guessing at the visitor's background puts the explanation inside her before she has said anything about herself. Asking which part of the route was unclear points at the letter, which the team can actually change.
The visitor wrote clearly about four unmarked doors. If she learned the team spent its time guessing about her instead, she might not bother writing next time.
What did the visitor's email actually say, and what did your question add to it?

decisions.setup: On Wednesday morning, the newer teammate sends written comments that identify details the meeting did not resolve about the visitor's route. The letter names the north entrance without an outside sign identifying north; bus passengers approach from the opposite side; and the web photograph shows a door replaced last year. Twenty minutes later, the experienced teammate replies to everyone: “Good points, but this is the kind of thing to raise in the meeting. People who care about this speak up in the room.” The team lead has not responded, and the decision about the letter remains open until Friday. You need to consider both the useful information in the comments and the expectation expressed in the reply.
decisions.prompt: How do you respond to the thread?

choices.text: Stay out of the thread so it does not turn into an argument, and message the newer teammate privately: “Don't worry about him, that's just how he is. Your comments were great.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate thanks you for the private message, but the experienced teammate's expectation remains unanswered in the thread the whole team received. The team lead eventually says she will review the comments, without addressing whether written input meets the needs of this decision. By Thursday, the draft includes the updated photograph while the point about arriving from the bus stop remains in the email. The newer teammate does not submit written comments on the next item, although the team has not examined what changed in their participation.

feedback.text: Supporting a colleague privately is kind, and avoiding a public disagreement feels safer. It helped your teammate feel better, but the expectation stated in the thread is still unanswered where the whole team saw it.
A stronger response addresses the content and the actual deadline in the thread, then checks in privately. This gives the responsible person a clear opportunity to use the information in the letter.
A short public line can do a lot: “Written comments work for me. The decision isn't until Friday. The bus-side point is worth adding.”

choices.text: Reply in the thread: the north-sign and bus-side points are useful, and written comments work for a Friday decision, so fold them in. Then check in with the newer teammate privately.
choices.consequence: Within an hour, the team lead replies, “Agreed. Friday is the deadline, and written comments work.” The experienced teammate responds later with a thumbs-up and a question about the bus stop, returning attention to the route information. During your private check-in, the newer teammate explains that the meeting moved too quickly to verify the map and writing allowed a careful check. They ask whether future agendas could arrive earlier, giving people more time to prepare useful comments before the discussion. The draft now includes the bus-side detail, connecting acceptance of the contribution with a concrete improvement in the letter.

feedback.text: You separated the real work need, useful input before Friday, from a familiar style of contributing, and you asked your teammate directly instead of guessing why. Build on it by suggesting the agenda change they raised, so the next newcomer does not have to ask.
For a newer teammate two months in, a public note about the content signals that careful written work counts here. A private check-in shows someone noticed without making them the topic.
Compared with simply reassuring your teammate in private, this response also addresses the expectation in front of the team, where it was stated.

choices.text: Reply to keep things moving: “Good points, and it does help to hear these in the meeting. Next time, just jump in so we can discuss them live.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate acknowledges your reply with a thumbs-up, while the team lead leaves the expectation about meeting participation unaddressed. The newer teammate responds, “Okay, will do,” and contributes nothing further to the thread about the revised letter. Nobody acts on the points about the north sign or the bus approach, even though both arrived before Friday's decision. Later that afternoon, the newer teammate stops you in the hallway, creating an opportunity to hear an explanation that the thread did not provide.

feedback.text: The team needed useful input before Friday, and your teammate delivered it. Backing a speak-in-the-room rule treats one style as the measure of commitment. A stronger reply addresses what they found and whether written comments meet the need.
To the newer teammate, this thread may read as: careful work gets criticized for its format. That lesson can follow a newcomer into supervision and the assignments they are offered.
Where did you learn that speaking up in the room shows you care? Does it fit every useful way of contributing?

choices.text: Message the experienced teammate privately to calm things down: “Go easy on our new teammate. They probably come from a background where people don't speak up in meetings, so writing felt safer.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate replies, “Oh, I didn't realize. I'll keep that in mind,” and softens the tone of his next message. The immediate tension eases, but he now holds an explanation for the written comments that the newer teammate never supplied. Before Friday's decision, he suggests to the team lead that someone else present next time because the newer colleague may be uncomfortable presenting. After hearing about that suggestion secondhand, the newer teammate approaches you near the elevators to discuss the explanation and its effect. Your attempt to help has now influenced an opportunity beyond the original exchange about comments on the letter.

feedback.text: You wanted to protect your teammate, and the tone did soften. But the explanation came from a guess about a group, not from the person. Asking them directly, and addressing whether written comments meet the need, would not leave a new label behind.
From the newer teammate's side, a colleague has explained their behavior to others using an identity, without asking. It has already shaped who gets the next presentation.
What did the newer teammate actually do, and what reason did you add to it?

decisions.setup: That afternoon, the experienced teammate shares a draft response in the team chat: “Thank you for your feedback. We have confirmed the address in our letter is correct. If you need help finding us, please call.” The team lead reacts with a thumbs-up, but the response has not yet been sent to the visitor. Rereading her email, you notice that she described difficulty choosing among four doors rather than uncertainty about the building's address. There is still time to raise that distinction before the draft becomes the team's answer to her concern.
decisions.prompt: Do you say anything about the draft reply?

choices.text: Post in the chat: “I reread her email. She found the building; it was the door she couldn't find. Could the reply ask which door she tried?”
choices.consequence: After a few minutes, the experienced teammate replies, “Huh, you're right. I read it fast.” He revises the response to ask which door the visitor tried first and what sign or detail would have helped. The team lead reopens the tracker item and shares the appointment letter for comments before a decision on Friday. The newer teammate acknowledges your message and privately adds, “Glad you said that. The north entrance thing always confused me too.” Returning to the visitor's words has reopened the practical question and created room for another colleague's relevant knowledge.

feedback.text: You went back to the visitor's actual words and offered your teammate a way to adjust without losing face. That is a recovery in real time. Next time, try raising the distinction in the meeting itself, while the whole team is there to hear it.
For the experienced teammate, a specific, friendly pointer to what the email said is much easier to act on than being told he got it wrong.

choices.text: Let it go. The experienced teammate has handled this letter for years, the meeting already decided, and reopening it now could leave him feeling second-guessed in front of the team lead.
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate sends the response without revising its explanation of the address or asking about the entrance problem. The following morning, the visitor replies, “I know the address is right. I said I couldn't find the door.” The team lead reopens the item, circulates the appointment letter as a draft and requests comments before Friday's decision. The review can now proceed, but the visitor has had to repeat information already present in her original account.

feedback.text: Deferring to an experienced colleague and a meeting decision is a very common choice, and it often feels like the respectful one. Here it let an answer to the wrong question reach the person who raised the concern.
A low-key way in next time: “Quick check before this goes. I think her point was about the door, not the address. Worth a question back to her?”

decisions.setup: The newer teammate stops you in the hallway to explain why they sent written comments after the meeting. “Can I tell you something? I wrote my comments instead of talking because I needed to check the building map and the bus routes first. I didn't want to say something wrong about the entrances in front of everyone. And now it feels like people have decided something about me.” They wait for your response, giving you an opportunity to reconsider the expectation you supported in the team thread.
decisions.prompt: What do you say to the newer teammate?

choices.text: “I am so sorry. I really was just trying to help the thread move along. I hope you know I am on your side, and I would never want you to feel singled out.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate replies, “I know,” and the conversation closes politely without an agreement about what should change in the thread. Your concern about your own intentions feels settled, while the expectation that commitment requires speaking in the meeting remains uncorrected. The bus-side detail is still absent from the draft, so the information supplied in writing has not yet improved that part of the letter. In later exchanges, the newer teammate remains friendly but limits comments to short verbal contributions rather than offering the same kind of written review.

feedback.text: Your apology was sincere, but it centered your intention and asked your teammate for reassurance. Naming the specific mistaken reading, and fixing it where it traveled, would address what they actually raised.
Try: “I got that wrong. You were checking facts, not holding back. Can I correct what I said in the thread? What would you want said?” Short, specific and about the action.
Reaching for your good intentions when you learn you caused harm is one of the most common reactions there is. Notice the pull, then turn back to what you were just told.

choices.text: “Thank you for telling me. I got that wrong: it was about checking your facts, not speaking up. I'd like to correct what I said. What would you want said?”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate agrees to a correction and explains the point they want made: “Yes. Just that written comments are a real way to contribute.” You return to the thread to acknowledge that “just jump in” was the wrong response to useful comments received before Friday's decision. Your note identifies the north-sign and bus-side findings without sharing the colleague's private explanation for how they prepared the comments. The team lead commits to sending agendas a day ahead, while the experienced teammate asks a follow-up question about the bus stop. The draft then incorporates the bus-side detail, making the contribution visible in the work as well as in the discussion.

feedback.text: You named the specific thing you got wrong, did not ask for reassurance, and asked what your teammate wanted said before saying anything. Then you corrected it where the impression formed. How it lands for them is something you will learn over time. Keep the habit of asking what else needs correcting.

For the newer teammate, a correction that reaches the thread matters more than a private apology, because the thread is where the impression formed. Being asked first also leaves them in charge of what the team hears about their reasons.
