decisions.setup: Near the elevators, the newer teammate approaches you about the explanation you offered to the experienced colleague without checking it first. “Can I tell you something? I heard you told him I come from a background where people don't speak up. That isn't why I wrote my comments instead of talking. I needed to check the building map and the bus routes first. Now someone else is doing the next presentation, and it feels like people have decided something about me.” They wait for your response, while the explanation you passed along has already reached a decision about presenting.
decisions.prompt: What do you say to the newer teammate?

choices.text: “I am so sorry. I was only trying to get him to ease up on you. I hope you know I am on your side, and I never meant it as criticism.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate says, “I know,” and the exchange ends politely without correcting the explanation you gave to the experienced colleague. That colleague still believes the account you supplied, and the presentation remains assigned to someone else while the bus-side detail remains outside the draft. Your apology may explain your intention, but it has not reached the people whose understanding or decisions were shaped by the unsupported explanation. The newer teammate continues to be friendly while keeping subsequent contributions short and verbal, rather than repeating the earlier approach to written comments.

feedback.text: Your apology was sincere, but it centered your intention and asked your teammate for reassurance. Naming the guess you passed on, and correcting it with the person who heard it, would address what they actually raised.
Try: “I got that wrong. I guessed a reason and passed it on. I'd like to tell him it was my guess. Is that okay with you?” Short, specific and about the action.
Reaching for your good intentions when you learn you caused harm is one of the most common reactions there is. Notice the pull, then turn back to what you were just told.

choices.text: “Thank you for telling me. I got it wrong: I guessed a reason and passed it on. Can I tell him it was my guess? What else should I correct?”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate agrees and adds, “Tell him. And I'd like a fair shot at presenting.” You tell the experienced teammate directly that the reason you supplied was your own incorrect guess, not an explanation the newer colleague had given. You leave the colleague's actual reasons for them to share, rather than replacing one unauthorized account with another. The experienced teammate says he will tell the team lead about the colleague's interest in presenting, without promising a particular assignment. He also asks about the bus stop in the thread, and the revised draft incorporates that part of the route.

feedback.text: You named the specific guess you made, did not ask for reassurance, and took the correction to the experienced teammate, where the label had traveled. You let your teammate decide what else was said. How it lands for them is something you will learn over time. Keep asking what else needs correcting.
For the newer teammate, knowing the experienced teammate was told the reason was a guess matters more than a private apology, because that guess was already shaping who presents.

decisions.setup: By Friday, the revised letter identifies the visitor door through a visible feature: the blue awning facing the parking lot. An updated photograph accompanies the wording, but the team has also learned that no outside sign identifies a visitor entrance. Responsibility for building signs rests with facilities staff, so the letter team cannot approve a new sign on its own. The experienced teammate suggests closing the tracker item as feedback addressed and sending the visitor a note of thanks. Before deciding, the team lead asks how you would describe what has changed and what still needs attention.
decisions.prompt: What do you suggest for closing the loop?

choices.text: “The letter is fixed, so mark it closed, and send her a thank-you that lists exactly what changed in the letter, so she knows her email made a difference.”
choices.consequence: The tracker item is marked complete, and the visitor receives a clear note listing the improvements made to the appointment letter. However, no one is assigned to send the sign request or ask whether the new wording would have resolved the visitor's difficulty. Two months later, front-desk staff mention that visitors continue asking which entrance to use, but the team does not connect this information with the closed item. The record accurately reflects a completed revision while leaving the effectiveness of that revision and the separate signage responsibility unexamined.

feedback.text: Revising the letter was a real action, and listing the changes for the visitor was a good touch. Whether visitors can now find the door is a separate question that needs its own evidence. Keeping that question open, and naming who owns the sign, would have caught the gap.
Closing an item feels like progress, and tidy trackers help teams function. The risk is treating a finished task as proof that the barrier is gone.
What would you need to hear from visitors to say the door problem is actually solved?

choices.text: “Tell her what changed and what went to facilities, ask if the new wording would have helped, and keep ‘does it work?’ open in the tracker.”
choices.consequence: The team lead asks the experienced teammate to send the sign request to facilities and explain that referral in the response to the visitor. The reply describes the letter revision and asks whether the new wording would have helped her identify the correct entrance. A week later, she explains that the blue-awning detail would help, but a tree hides the awning from the sidewalk until someone approaches the door. That account provides another practical condition to examine, without establishing that every visitor experiences the route in the same way. The team now has a specific follow-up question and a record that distinguishes its completed action from the effect still being checked.

feedback.text: You kept three things apart: what the team changed, what belongs to someone else, and whether it actually works for visitors. Asking the visitor directly is what turned up the hidden awning. Set a date to check the sign request, too.
For the visitor, an account of what changed and a further question make the team's response visible. Whether she feels heard or chooses to contribute again remains hers to say.
Consider adding one line to the tracker for the next review: ask the front desk whether visitors still ask which door to use.

choices.text: “Let's tell her a new Visitors sign is going up. She circled the building twice, and a firm promise shows her we took it seriously.”
choices.consequence: The visitor thanks the team for promising a sign, before facilities staff have assessed or approved the proposed change. When the experienced teammate contacts them, facilities explains that exterior signs require review and may take months if they are approved. The team lead must now decide how to correct the promise and explain what the team actually has authority to deliver. Although the revised letter remains a useful action, the unsupported commitment has created an additional issue in the team's relationship with the visitor.

feedback.text: You wanted the visitor to know her concern mattered, which is right. A promise about a sign the team does not control can undercut that trust. Saying the request has gone to the people responsible, and what the team did change, is honest and still shows follow-through.
If the sign never appears, the visitor may remember the promise more than the improved letter.
Next time, separate the two in your reply: “Here is what changed. Here is what has been asked of the people who handle signs, and when you can expect to hear more.”

choices.text: “She clearly knows what visitors need. Let's thank her and ask her to review all our building letters, since she can spot problems we would miss.”
choices.consequence: The visitor welcomes the revision but explains that she has neither the time nor the knowledge of other buildings to review their letters. The team leaves those reviews waiting on her, transferring responsibility beyond the specific experience she originally offered to help explain. Meanwhile, nobody asks whether the revised wording would have addressed the difficulty she encountered at this building's entrance. Attention has moved to a larger request without resolving the narrower question for which the visitor already has relevant firsthand knowledge.

feedback.text: Valuing her knowledge is a good instinct. Asking her to review everything, though, turns one person's useful account into staff work, and makes her stand in for every visitor.
A stronger move asks the visitor about the one thing she knows, whether the new wording would have helped her, and keeps the review of other letters with the team.
When someone raises a concern in your work, how do you tell the difference between inviting their knowledge and handing them your job?

practiced: Keeping an accurate fact and a person's experience side by side when they answer different questions
Asking the person what went wrong instead of guessing about their background
Separating a real work need from a familiar style of contributing
Naming a specific mistaken reading and correcting it where it traveled
Asking the person what they want said before correcting something about them
Telling people what changed, what did not, and who is responsible for the rest
Keeping the question of whether a change works open until there is evidence
this_week: Reread one recent concern from the public or a colleague and write down, word for word, what they actually said.
Before your next meeting, ask whether written input before the decision would meet the need as well as speaking in the room.
Pick one item marked done in your work and ask whether anyone has checked if it works for the people it was for.
When you reply to someone who raised a concern, tell them what changed, what did not, and who holds the rest.

simulations.intro: If you work the front desk or the phones, you are often the first person someone meets at DHS. I know how easy it is to trust the email, the file or the usual routine over what the person in front of you is saying. In this version, you greet a visitor who could not find the door, set up his next visit and decide what to do about the directions.
simulations.title: The Front Desk
simulations.learner_role: You are a Customer Service Specialist at the front desk of a DHS building. You greet visitors, book meetings with program staff, arrange interpreters and other supports, and keep visitor records up to date. You can propose changes to the confirmation email, but the template belongs to the person or area responsible for building communications.
simulations.background: Every visitor receives a confirmation email giving the street address and meeting time, without identifying which entrance the public should use. Four sets of doors face the street, but the public entrance is not marked where someone approaching from the sidewalk would see it. Today a visitor is expected to meet a program staff member about a service his family uses, while your coworker covers the desk with you. The next visitor is due in twenty minutes, creating a practical limit on the time available to respond to an unexpected difficulty.

decisions.setup: The visitor arrives twenty-five minutes late and out of breath after walking around the building twice to find an entrance. He explains that the email gave the address, but each door he tried was locked or marked for staff only. Your coworker quietly says, “The address is right there on the email,” while the program staff member has another meeting in twenty minutes. You need to respond to the difficulty he describes and establish what options are still available for today’s appointment.
decisions.prompt: What do you do first?

choices.text: Agree that the address is correct, show the visitor exactly where it is on the email so he has it for next time, then check whether the staff member can still see him today.
choices.consequence: The visitor replies, “I know the address,” and sounds more frustrated than when he first approached the desk for help. You have not yet contacted the staff member, so the time remaining before her next meeting continues to narrow.

feedback.text: The address was correct, and that was never his question. The readings use almost this exact moment: an accurate address and a usable route are different things. Asking which part of the directions did not help would have found the gap.
The visitor followed the address but still could not enter the building. Repeating that information leaves his specific difficulty unanswered and may imply that he caused the problem.
When you walk through the right door every day, it is hard to picture not finding it. That is insider knowledge, and it is exactly what a newcomer does not have.

choices.text: Say you are sorry it was hard to find and ask which part of the directions did not help. Call the staff member about the time left, and let the visitor choose.
choices.consequence: The visitor explains that the email did not identify the public entrance and that the locked doors appeared to be the front entrance. After you call, the staff member offers fifteen minutes today, which he chooses to use before arranging a longer follow-up. You record his description of the route: “Could not tell which doors are public. Tried two locked sets first.”

feedback.text: You heard the specific difficulty instead of defending the email, and you gave him a real choice inside a real limit. Writing down his exact words means his knowledge can travel to the people who can fix the directions.
To your coworker, the email looked complete. The visitor’s account shows her something about the building she cannot see from behind the desk.

choices.text: Tell the visitor not to worry and that it was not his fault: the staff member will still see him for the full hour, and you will let her know he is here.
choices.consequence: The visitor initially relaxes, but the staff member then explains that only fifteen minutes remain before her next scheduled meeting. He looks toward you after hearing that limit, leaving you to correct a promise made before checking the time available.

feedback.text: Wanting to fix it for him was kind. The promise came before checking. Calling the staff member first, then giving the visitor the real options, would have kept your word good.
Try: “Let me call the staff member right now and find out what time she has. Then you can decide what works best.”

choices.text: Explain this desk’s practice: visitors more than fifteen minutes late reschedule, so staff calendars stay on track. Apologize for the trouble, and offer the visitor the next opening.
choices.consequence: The visitor explains that he reached the building on time and picks up his coat after hearing that he must reschedule. The staff member still does not know he has arrived, and no one has recorded which entrances prevented him from reaching the desk.

feedback.text: This desk’s lateness practice may serve a real purpose, like protecting staff schedules, but it is a habit of the desk, not a requirement handed down. The stronger choice checks what is actually possible today and asks why he was late before applying it.
Which of the front desk’s rules come from a requirement, and which are habits that grew up around one?
From the visitor’s side, the building kept him out, and then the desk did too.

decisions.setup: The visitor wants a longer follow-up next week, and the booking form asks whether an interpreter will be needed for the meeting. A visitor record completed by someone else years ago lists a preferred language other than English, although he has been speaking English with you. Your coworker says, “It’s in his file. Just book the interpreter,” before anyone asks what communication arrangements he wants for this visit. He also mentions that standing for a long time is difficult, without giving a reason or asking to discuss his health.
decisions.prompt: How do you set up his next visit?

choices.text: Ask how he wants to communicate and whether he wants an interpreter, in which language. Offer a seat near the entrance and a call when it is time, without asking why.
choices.consequence: The visitor wants to meet in English, with his wife joining by phone and an interpreter supporting her in the language listed on the form. He accepts the seat near the entrance and a call when the staff member is ready, without discussing why standing is difficult. Booking takes three additional minutes because the arrangements now reflect the preferences he described for the people attending this particular meeting.

feedback.text: You asked instead of reading his needs from a file, from how he speaks or from a comment about standing. You also offered support without making a reason the price of it. His answer was something no one could have guessed: the interpreter was for someone else.
Keep the question open-ended and the same for everyone: “Is there anything that would make this visit work better for you?” It lets people tell you what matters without being singled out.

choices.text: Book the interpreter in the language from the file, as your coworker suggests. It is in his record, and it is better to have one there and not need it than the reverse.
choices.consequence: When you read back the confirmation, the visitor frowns and asks, “An interpreter? For me?” He then asks what else the file says about him, while the question of who else might join the meeting remains unasked.

feedback.text: The record offers information worth checking, but it does not establish the visitor’s current preferences or who will attend this appointment. Asking about those details helps you arrange language support that fits the visit.

Ask who will attend and how each person wants to communicate, including whether an interpreter is needed and in which language. A question about the visitor alone would not necessarily identify his wife’s participation.

choices.text: Skip the interpreter and leave the language field blank. He clearly speaks English well, the old form is out of date, and booking one he does not need wastes a slot.
choices.consequence: After you book the meeting without language support, the visitor asks whether his wife can join by phone with an interpreter. The arrangements do not currently provide for either request, so the booking will need further attention before the visit.

feedback.text: You were right not to trust the old file. The stronger move replaces one guess with a question, not with a different guess based on how he speaks.
When you decide someone does not need a support, what are you usually basing it on?

choices.text: Ask the visitor, kindly, what health condition makes standing hard, so you can note it for the staff member and staff can plan the right support for his visit.
choices.consequence: The visitor replies, “I’d rather not get into that,” and the conversation becomes quiet at the public desk beside your coworker. A seat has not yet been offered, and the question about communication preferences for the next visit remains unresolved.

feedback.text: A seat near the entrance and a call when the staff member is ready do not need a diagnosis. Practical help should not depend on sharing a personal history.
From the visitor’s side, a passing comment has turned into a health question at a public desk, in front of a coworker.
Offer the support and let the person choose: “Would a seat near the entrance help, with a call when the staff member is ready?”

decisions.setup: The appointment time is set, but the confirmation template still provides only the address and the visitor record retains the old language entry. You remember at least two other visitors who arrived late this month after struggling to find the entrance to the building. Those accounts suggest a recurring problem to examine, although they do not establish how every visitor experiences the directions. Consider what you can update directly, what needs review by the person or area responsible, and what further information would help assess a change.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now that the visit is set?

choices.text: Update the visitor’s record, send his words and a clearer entrance line to the person or area responsible for the template, and ask the next visitors whether they found the door.
choices.consequence: You confirm the record with the visitor, identifying English for him and a telephone interpreter for the person joining this appointment. The communications team adds a sentence identifying the glass doors facing the parking lot, while a request for clearer signage goes to facilities. You send the revised directions to the visitor and ask subsequent visitors about their experience over the next two weeks. Most describe finding the entrance easily, but one reports trying the side doors first, which you pass to the communications team. These responses provide initial evidence about the change and identify a remaining difficulty, without establishing that the directions work for everyone.

feedback.text: You followed the problem past the desk: the record, the template and the next visitors. And you kept your claim honest. A clearer line is an action; whether people can find the door is a separate question you went and asked.
The visitor who still tried the side doors matters. One improvement does not settle everyone’s experience, and you kept listening after the fix.

choices.text: Edit the confirmation template yourself to name the glass doors facing the parking lot, so this does not happen again, and tell your supervisor the problem is fixed.
choices.consequence: Although your revised wording identifies the entrance more clearly, the communications team restores the previous version because changes require its review. Your supervisor has already described the problem as fixed in a meeting, while the visitor record still contains the old language entry.

feedback.text: You identified a useful revision, but the person or area responsible must review it before it becomes the shared template. After approval, check visitors’ experiences to learn whether the change helps and what remains difficult.
What is the difference between changing the email and knowing the change helped?

choices.text: Add “visitor confused by directions” to the visitor’s record, so the next person at the desk knows to explain the entrance to him, and move on to the next visitor.
choices.consequence: The next employee opening the record sees a description of the visitor as confused, without the specific information about which doors he tried. The template remains unchanged, and another visitor arrives late the following week after struggling to find the entrance.

feedback.text: “Confused” puts the problem in the visitor. His account put it in the directions. Compare: “Could not tell which doors are public.” One labels the visitor; the other names the gap.
Picture the visitor’s next visit. Whoever greets him may now speak to him slowly and simply, because of one word in a record.

choices.text: Update the visitor’s record and send him a personal email with clear directions to the glass doors. Leave the template alone, since templates belong to communications and are not part of your job.
choices.consequence: The visitor thanks you for the individual directions and arrives on time the following week, giving you useful information about that appointment. However, other visitors still receive the original template because the person or area responsible has not received the suggested change.

feedback.text: You did right by the visitor. The stronger choice also passes his account to the person or area responsible, because the barrier is in a routine every visitor meets.

When you notice a recurring problem, share the specific accounts and a suggested change with the person or area responsible. Follow applicable privacy procedures when deciding what details to include.

decisions.setup: The visitor responds, “I was here. I just couldn’t find the door,” distinguishing the time he reached the building from the time he reached your desk. Your coworker looks toward you, while there is still an opportunity to ask about the route and check the staff member’s remaining time.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Say “That makes sense. Which doors did you try?” Listen, call the staff member about the time left, and let him choose how to use it.
choices.consequence: The visitor describes the two locked entrances, and the staff member confirms that a brief meeting is still possible today. He chooses that option and a longer follow-up, while you record which doors he tried so the route can be examined.

feedback.text: You let his correction change your response, and you asked about the specific difficulty instead of repeating the address.
Your coworker heard it too. The visitor’s account is now something the whole desk knows.

choices.text: Apologize warmly for the trouble, tell him the building is confusing for a lot of people, and offer him the first open time on the staff member’s calendar.
choices.consequence: The visitor accepts a new appointment, while the brief opening in the staff member’s schedule goes unused because you have not checked it. No one records which doors he tried, leaving the specific difficulty unavailable to the people reviewing the directions.

feedback.text: The apology acknowledges the inconvenience without resolving the immediate options or the route problem. Asking which doors he tried and checking the staff member’s time would provide information for both decisions.
When someone reports a difficulty, pair the acknowledgment with a relevant question and an explanation of what you can do next.

choices.text: Point out the small sign by the parking lot, say most people find it without trouble, and suggest he look for it when he comes back next time.
choices.consequence: The visitor says he did not see the sign and offers no further detail during the remainder of the check-in. You have identified a feature familiar to staff without learning why it was not visible or useful along his route.

feedback.text: Most people finding it does not mean everyone can. One person’s account can show a gap that others found a way around.
When you defend a sign or a form, who are you picturing using it?

decisions.setup: The visitor’s response shows that an assumption shaped the proposed arrangements or that your question went beyond what he wanted to discuss. Because the follow-up is still a week away, there is time to ask about his preferences and revise the arrangements before the appointment.
decisions.prompt: How do you set it right?

choices.text: Ask the visitor how he wants to communicate, who will join and what would help. Change the booking to match, without asking for a reason.
choices.consequence: The visitor explains that the interpreter is for his wife, who will join by phone, and you revise the booking accordingly. He accepts the seat near the entrance and a call when the staff member is ready, thanking you for asking without requesting a personal explanation.

feedback.text: You replaced the assumption with his answer, and kept practical help separate from any personal explanation.
Ask the same supports question of every visitor, so no one is singled out by it.

choices.text: Fix the booking quietly: adjust what you set up, apologize for the mix-up, and ask nothing more, so the visitor is not put on the spot again.
choices.consequence: You adjust the arrangement and apologize, but nobody asks which communication options or practical supports would make the visit work better. Who will join, the language support needed and the seating arrangement therefore remain unsettled despite the changes to the booking.

feedback.text: Removing a wrong guess helps. Asking what he does want would have found the support that was actually needed.
What did you learn about the visitor just now, and what do you still not know?

choices.text: Explain where the setup came from: his visitor record and what the desk usually does, so he knows it was not personal and the desk followed its process.
choices.consequence: The visitor explains that someone else completed the record years ago without asking him about his preferences at that time. Your response has shifted the discussion toward why the desk used the record, leaving the arrangements for this visit unresolved.

feedback.text: Explaining where a decision came from is a natural reaction. It defends the booking instead of fixing it.
To the visitor, an old record is being taken over what he is saying in front of you.

practiced: Hearing a visitor’s specific difficulty instead of defending accurate directions
Checking what is possible before making a promise, then giving the person the choice
Asking how a person wants to communicate instead of reading it from a file or from how they speak
Offering practical support without making a personal reason the price of it
Writing down a person’s own words so their knowledge can reach the person or area responsible
Checking how a change works for visitors and using their accounts to identify remaining difficulties
this_week: Ask the next three visitors who arrive late what part of getting here was hard, and write down their words.
Before booking an interpreter or support from a record, ask the visitor what they want for this visit.
Read the confirmation email as someone who has never been to the building, and send one suggested change to the person or area responsible.

simulations.intro: If you choose categories, run the numbers or write findings, your words travel further than you do. I have seen one sentence in a report become the way a whole group is described for years. In this version, you write a finding, run a results session with community partners and decide what the report can honestly claim.
simulations.title: What the Numbers Can Say
simulations.learner_role: You are a research analyst in a DHS research and evaluation unit. You choose how results are grouped, write the findings and their limits, and present them to the program that asked for the study. The program’s decisions, and the data rules your unit follows, belong to the person or area responsible.
simulations.background: A DHS program overseeing in-home support services requested an analysis of a statewide survey about access to case managers and understanding service plans. Your report groups responses by race, ethnicity and preferred language, using a survey offered online and by telephone in English and one other language. The paper version was available only in English, and far fewer completed surveys came from people whose preferred language was not English. The program manager needs findings for a legislative report in three weeks, with a community-partner results session scheduled for next week. Three people representing different community organizations have agreed to participate, providing an opportunity to examine interpretations and limitations before the report is finalized.

decisions.setup: A colleague’s draft states, “People whose preferred language is not English were less engaged with the survey and less satisfied with their case managers.” The data establish that fewer surveys were returned from that group and that, among respondents, a lower proportion reported understanding their service plan. The methods checklist records “Language access: yes,” without distinguishing the languages and formats available to different potential respondents. Consider whether the draft accurately describes the measures collected and what the findings can establish about the people who did not respond.
decisions.prompt: How do you write the finding?

choices.text: Keep the colleague’s sentence. It is a fair short summary of both results, the program asked for plain findings, and the Legislature report is three weeks out.
choices.consequence: The program manager plans to quote the sentence in a briefing, extending its interpretation beyond the analysis where the wording began. A partner reviewing the advance copy responds, “Less engaged? The survey was never offered in the language most of our members read.” The draft attributes a disposition to potential respondents without evidence that distinguishes that explanation from barriers in the survey itself.

feedback.text: “Fewer surveys were returned” is an observation. “Less engaged” adds a reason. The readings use this exact distinction: the form not returned is a fact; “not interested” is an inference. The stronger draft keeps them apart.
For the people behind those numbers, “less engaged” becomes a description of them in a legislative document, when the barrier may have been the survey itself.
In your last report, which words described what the data showed, and which supplied a motive?

choices.text: Report what the data shows, fewer returns and a lower share who understand their plan, with counts and limits. Name the survey’s two languages. List possible reasons as open questions.
choices.consequence: The revised finding distinguishes returned surveys, reported understanding and collection limits without assigning an explanation to people who did not respond. When the program manager asks why the reasons remain questions, you explain that several possibilities fit the observations, including limitations in survey reach. She agrees to discuss those possibilities with the partners rather than presenting the first interpretation as an established conclusion.

feedback.text: You kept respondent findings, collection limitations and possible explanations distinct, allowing additional evidence to challenge the first interpretation. Apply the same distinction to the checklist by specifying which languages and formats were offered.
When you list open questions, write them so the answer could change your interpretation, for example: “Did people receive the survey in a language they read well?”

choices.text: Keep the observed facts, and add context from a published community brief saying some communities are less comfortable rating professionals, so readers understand why the gap in the results might appear.
choices.consequence: A partner reviewing the draft points out that the community brief concerns a study conducted in another state with a different population. She describes people who regularly evaluate services when the questions are offered in a usable format, challenging the explanation attached to your findings. The brief provides background for further inquiry, but its findings have been applied to respondents and nonrespondents it did not study.

feedback.text: Reaching for published context is a good research habit. The readings draw the line here: a brief can prepare better questions, but it cannot supply the answer for a person or a group in your data. Keep a source’s time, place and purpose visible.

Compare using the brief to write a question, such as “Is comfort rating professionals part of this gap?”, with using it as the answer. The first invites partners to correct you; the second closes the inquiry.

choices.text: Remove the non-English results from the main tables. The numbers are small, small numbers can mislead, and your unit’s caution about unstable estimates points the same way.
choices.consequence: The revised tables no longer show results for the group least reached by the survey, without explaining that omission in the report. Reading the totals, the program manager concludes that no meaningful difference by language exists, although the analysis does not establish that conclusion. A partner reviewing the advance copy asks what happened to the experiences of the people her organization serves.

feedback.text: Caution about small numbers is sound, and your unit’s small-number rules still apply. The stronger choice reports what can be shown within those rules and says plainly whose experience the data could not reach.
When a group drops out of a table, where does the reader learn that it happened and why?

decisions.setup: At the results session, the program manager asks you to “walk them through it and get their sign-off by the end of the hour.” The first partner questions a combined category that groups communities with different service experiences, while the second describes surveys received in a language people read poorly. The third partner has not yet spoken, leaving her interpretation of the findings unknown to the group at this point. Data collection is complete and the reporting deadline is fixed, but some decisions about presentation, limitations and future collection remain open.
decisions.prompt: How do you run the session?

choices.text: Say what is fixed, the data and the date, and what is still open: wording, limits, how categories are shown and the next survey. Then ask what they see.
choices.consequence: You explain that partners can contribute their knowledge without being asked to represent everyone in a community or endorse the complete report. The first suggests a note explaining what the combined category conceals, while the second offers language for describing collection limits. The third questions whether asking about understanding a written plan assumes receipt of a document she rarely sees people receive. Her observation introduces a question about the survey measure itself that the research team had not previously raised.

feedback.text: You clarified the decisions available for discussion and received a question about what the survey measure assumes. That contribution can inform further analysis without being treated as proof about every person’s experience.
From the partners’ side, an hour of their time now has a purpose they can see. They were asked to inform choices, not to approve a finished product.
Before the session ends, read back what you heard and which part of the report each point could affect. It shows the input landed somewhere.
If someone has not spoken, offer a route that does not put them on the spot: “Anyone who would rather send thoughts after today can write to me by Friday.”

choices.text: Present the findings as written and ask for sign-off by the end of the hour, as the program manager asked. Log every concern the partners raise so it shapes the next survey.
choices.consequence: The first partner says she cannot endorse categories that obscure differences among the people her organization serves, while the second questions the meeting’s purpose. Forty minutes pass without identifying a decision their input can affect in the current report, despite its remaining scope for revision. Their concerns are recorded for a survey two years away, leaving the present interpretation and limitations unchanged.

feedback.text: Asking for approval of a finished draft is a request for endorsement, not partnership. The readings describe this exactly: a contribution heard, but given no relevant choice to affect.
Deadlines push toward sign-off. That pressure is real. But some things in this report are still open, and saying which ones is what makes the hour worth the partners’ time.

choices.text: Agree on the spot to split the combined category and re-run every table for this report, so the partners can see right away that their concerns are taken seriously.
choices.consequence: After promising separate tables, you consult the codebook and discover that the survey did not collect the detail needed for that breakdown. Your unit’s small-number rules would also limit disclosure in many proposed tables, requiring further review even where more detailed data were available. You must now correct the commitment and explain which revisions remain possible within the collected information and applicable rules.

feedback.text: Responding fast felt like respect, but the promise came before checking what was possible. The stronger move separates the real limit, what the data holds, from what can still change, like how the category is labeled and explained.
Try: “I don’t know yet whether the data can be split that way. I will check, and I will tell you by Friday what is possible and what is not.”

choices.text: Ask the first partner to explain how people in her community feel about their case managers, so the report can include a community view alongside the numbers.
choices.consequence: The first partner explains that she can describe what members have told her, but their experiences and views are not uniform. The third partner remains silent, while the discussion shifts toward obtaining a community-wide opinion through a single participant. That request goes beyond the interpretation and firsthand information the partner has offered to contribute to the analysis.

feedback.text: From the first partner’s side, she came to help interpret data and was asked to stand in for a whole community. One person’s account can inform the analysis; it cannot represent everyone.
What question could you ask the first partner about the data that uses what she knows without making her a spokesperson?

decisions.setup: Two weeks later, the program manager notes that an English-only outreach letter was sent halfway through the survey period, with no complaints received afterward. She proposes the conclusion, “Outreach improved understanding of service plans for all groups,” although the survey has not established the letter’s effect. You also owe the partners an explanation of how their input affected the report and which suggestions could not be incorporated.
decisions.prompt: What does the report say, and what do you tell the partners?

choices.text: Report the letter as an action whose effect is not yet known, and say whose experience the survey missed. Tell partners what their input changed and what did not.
choices.consequence: The program manager initially questions the limitation, then agrees that an English-only letter and an absence of complaints do not establish improved understanding across groups. The report describes the outreach action, its unmeasured effect and the limits of the survey’s reach and interpretation. Your follow-up identifies each partner suggestion, what changed, and why certain tables could not be separated under the available data and disclosure rules. The second partner replies that this is the first study to explain what happened afterward, providing feedback about the follow-up itself.

feedback.text: You distinguished the outreach action, its unmeasured effect and the absence of complaints. The follow-up makes the use of partner input visible, while the quality of the partnership still depends on participants’ experience and subsequent work.
Think of a legislator reading the report. A claim of improvement for all groups would invite a decision the data cannot support. Your version lets them see what is known and what is not.

choices.text: Use the program manager’s sentence. It is her program’s report, the outreach letter probably helped, and with the Legislature deadline close, a clear message is what she needs.
choices.consequence: The report proceeds with the improvement claim, while the partners find that their concerns about interpretation and reach are absent from the published account. When the next survey shows a similar difference, the program must explain why its earlier report described an improvement that had not been established.

feedback.text: No complaints does not show the barrier disappeared. The readings say missing feedback cannot be labeled satisfaction. The stronger draft names the outreach as an action and its effect as unknown.
Deferring to the program owner is often right on program choices. The wording of an evidence claim, though, is part of your work, and accuracy is the thing you bring.
Try offering the program manager a sentence she can live with: “The program sent an outreach letter during the survey period; the survey cannot yet show its effect.”

choices.text: Remove any statement about outreach, and say the data cannot support conclusions about anything for people whose preferred language is not English, given how few surveys returned.
choices.consequence: The report replaces the specific findings and partner contributions with a general statement that the data cannot support any conclusion for the group. The program manager loses both the observed information about respondents and the explanation of collection limits that could inform further work.

feedback.text: The survey provides information about respondents and its own reach, even though it does not establish the experiences of everyone who did not respond. Report what can be supported within the unit’s rules and explain the remaining uncertainty.
What can this data honestly say, even if it cannot say everything?

choices.text: Write the report accurately, naming the letter as an action with an unknown effect, and leave it to the program manager, who owns the partner relationships, to decide whether and when to contact them.
choices.consequence: The report distinguishes the outreach action from its unknown effect, but no one sends the partners an account of how their contributions were used. Months later, the first partner’s organization declines another invitation, explaining that it never heard what happened after the previous study. Accurate analysis has been retained, while the promised communication about participation remains incomplete.

feedback.text: The report itself is sound. The stronger choice also closes the loop, because an opportunity to speak does not show the concern informed anything unless people hear what happened.
Draft the partner note yourself and offer it to the program manager: what was heard, what changed, what did not and why, who to contact next.

decisions.setup: A partner’s comment on the advance copy gives you a reason to examine the finding before next week’s results session. The draft remains open to revision, allowing you to distinguish what the observed responses establish from the additional explanation the wording supplies.
decisions.prompt: What do you change?

choices.text: Rewrite the finding as what was observed, add the survey’s language limits, and turn the reasons into open questions for the session.
choices.consequence: The revised draft reports the returned surveys and respondent findings within the unit’s disclosure rules, identifying where results cannot be shown. It names the available survey languages and presents three possible explanations as questions, which the program manager agrees to discuss with partners.

feedback.text: You let a second look change the finding, not just its tone. That is self-examination applied to your own draft.
Keep a short list of words that add motive, like “engaged”, “reluctant” or “uninterested”, and search your drafts for them.

choices.text: Keep the structure but soften the claim: change “were less engaged” to “may have been less engaged,” and add a line noting the survey’s language limits.
choices.consequence: The added limitation makes the collection constraint visible, but the main sentence still directs readers toward an untested explanation about people’s engagement. Reviewing the revision, the partner replies that the same attributed motive remains despite the more tentative wording.

feedback.text: “May have been” softens the inference but keeps it. The stronger rewrite removes the motive and reports what was observed.
If the survey had been offered in more languages, would the finding still read this way?

choices.text: Keep the draft as it is. This is how findings are usually written, and the partners can raise their concerns at the session next week, where there is time.
choices.consequence: The partners arrive having read the unchanged description of engagement, and the opening twenty minutes focus on challenging that interpretation. Time available for examining other findings is reduced because the concern raised on the advance copy was deferred.

feedback.text: From the partners’ side, the session now starts with defending their communities instead of interpreting results.
Standard phrasing feels safe because it is familiar. Familiar is not the same as accurate.

decisions.setup: The second partner asks, “So what are we here for?” and the program manager looks toward you for a response. Twenty minutes remain in the session, leaving time to clarify which decisions the partners can still inform before the report is finalized.
decisions.prompt: How do you answer?

choices.text: Answer plainly: the data and date are fixed; wording, limits, how categories are shown and the next survey are open. Then ask about each one.
choices.consequence: The first partner proposes a note about the combined category, and the third raises her question about whether people received written service plans. The remaining discussion produces three proposed revisions and one question to investigate, connecting participants’ knowledge with decisions still open in the report.

feedback.text: You answered a hard question with an honest map of what can change. That is what made the remaining twenty minutes useful.

The partner explicitly asked what the session was intended to accomplish. Answering that question clarified the available decisions without requiring an inference about whether his tone reflected hostility.

choices.text: Apologize that the purpose was not clear, and promise a follow-up email by Friday with next steps, what can still change and what cannot.
choices.consequence: The partners accept the promised follow-up, but the session closes without connecting their observations to specific choices in the current report. The email must now clarify the scope and invite responses that could have been discussed during the remaining meeting time.

feedback.text: A follow-up is useful, but the open choices could have been named now, while people were in the room to respond.
When asked “what are we here for?”, try answering in the moment with one fixed item and one open item.

choices.text: Give the partners the draft and ask them to rewrite the parts they disagree with before the report goes in, so the final wording is truly theirs.
choices.consequence: The partners receive a request to rewrite material they were invited to discuss, without a prior agreement about that additional work or compensation. Two send edits and one does not reply, leaving you responsible for the analysis and for clarifying how their contributions will be used.

feedback.text: Partnership values what people know without assigning them staff work. The analysis stays yours; their input informs it.
What is the difference between asking for someone’s knowledge and asking them to do your job?

practiced: Separating an observation in the data from a reason the writer added
Using a published brief to write a better question, not to explain people in the data
Reporting a group the data reached poorly instead of letting it drop out of view
Telling partners what is fixed and what their input can still shape
Hearing one partner’s knowledge without asking them to speak for a whole community
Keeping an action, its effect and missing feedback distinct in a finding
Telling partners what happened to their input, including what did not change and why
this_week: Read one finding you wrote recently and mark each word that describes what was observed and each word that supplies a motive.
Find one “yes” on a methods checklist and write one sentence on the evidence behind it.
Before your next results session, write down what is fixed and what is still open, and say both at the start.

simulations.intro: If you answer a call line or explain applications and notices, the information you provide can shape someone’s understanding of the next step. I have learned that a record and a person’s account can point to different explanations of the same event. In this version, you take a renewal call and decide what to ask, what the record establishes and what the next worker needs to know.
simulations.title: The Renewal Call
simulations.learner_role: You answer a DHS health care eligibility call line. You explain notices, check what a case shows, tell people what they can do next and write the case note. Some outcomes are yours to explain but not yours to decide; those belong to the person or area responsible for the eligibility decision.
simulations.background: A caller contacts a DHS health care eligibility line about a notice stating that coverage closed because her renewal was not returned. Her adult son joins the call, while an earlier contact note on your screen reads, “Client unresponsive. Declined interpreter.” The caller pauses before answering and speaks carefully, without yet explaining which language or communication arrangements she prefers for this conversation. Six people are waiting in the queue, creating pressure to move quickly while you establish what help she is requesting. The notice, case status and available renewal steps described here belong to this fictional case; current program and privacy procedures govern actual calls.

decisions.setup: The caller says, “I never understood this letter. My son helps me with these things,” before he begins explaining the notice for her. The earlier note remains visible on your screen, but you have not asked the caller how she wants to communicate or participate. Before discussing case details with her son, you also need to establish the permission required under the applicable privacy procedure.
decisions.prompt: How do you open the conversation?

choices.text: Offer an interpreter right away in the language you guess from her accent. The earlier note is probably out of date, and her English seems slow and careful.
choices.consequence: The caller pauses and says, “I don’t speak that language,” after which her son laughs and she begins giving shorter answers. You apologize and ask which language she uses, recognizing that the offer was based on an assumption about her accent rather than her stated preference.

feedback.text: Reaching for an interpreter is a caring instinct, and many people on call lines do it. The trouble is where the choice came from: an accent cannot tell you a person’s language, needs or preference. The readings are plain on this: do not infer meaning from identity, an accent or appearance.
Compare this with simply asking: “Which language would you like to use today? I can bring in an interpreter if that helps.” Same care, but the caller makes the choice.
Think about how this lands for the caller. She has already been told by a letter that she missed something. Now a guess about who she is arrives before any question about what she needs.

choices.text: Ask the caller which language she wants, whether she wants a free interpreter, and whether her son should help. Check permission before discussing her case with him.
choices.consequence: The caller chooses English with her son present, and you confirm the required permission before discussing her case with him on this call. You explain that a professional interpreter remains available at no cost if she wants one, including for unfamiliar terms. She then explains that the earlier interpreter offer concerned a language she does not speak, providing context absent from the previous note. Her son pauses while she answers the next question, allowing you to hear directly what she wants help understanding.

feedback.text: You asked before you assumed. The note, the pause and her son’s quick answer all pointed toward a story, and you let the caller tell her own instead. You also kept a free interpreter open to her for the whole call, so a family member does not have to carry the hard words. Build on it: when a note gives a reason, treat it as one possible reading until the person confirms it.

The caller’s stated preference now guides the conversation, and the permission check establishes the basis for involving her son. Her explanation also gives the next worker information that the earlier note did not contain.

choices.text: Read the note, then explain the renewal and the letter clearly and in full, step by step, so nothing is missed. Then ask whether she has any questions before you go on.
choices.consequence: After the complete explanation, the caller asks, “So what do I send?” while her son identifies the notice wording as the unresolved problem. Ten minutes have passed without establishing which part of the letter she could not use, despite several affirmative responses during your explanation.

feedback.text: The explanation may be accurate while failing to address the caller’s specific difficulty. Asking which part was hard to use gives you a way to focus the response without assuming that a nod or yes establishes understanding.
When someone says “yes” over and over during an explanation, what do you usually take it to mean, and how could you check?
Next time, start with the person’s own words: “You said you never understood this letter. Which part was the hardest?” Then explain only that part first.

choices.text: Her son answers quickly and speaks easily, so direct your questions to him to save time for the six callers waiting. The caller can add anything he misses.
choices.consequence: Her son answers questions about income but guesses at the work hours, while you move to another question before the caller can respond. She interrupts to explain, “He doesn’t know my hours. I work two jobs,” correcting information that could otherwise enter the record. You have also not established the permission required to discuss her case with him, leaving an additional problem to address.

feedback.text: From where the caller sits, the call is now about her but no longer with her. You controlled who got to speak. That is role influence, even when the goal is speed.

A long queue pushes everyone to take the fastest voice on the line. That pressure is real. The readings ask you to notice who has room to shape the interaction, because the fastest voice is not always the person whose case it is.

Thank her son, then turn to the caller: “Would you like your son to help, or would you like to answer yourself? Either is fine.” Then check what the case rules need before you discuss details with him.

decisions.setup: For this fictional case, the record shows that the renewal can still be processed if the form and income proof arrive by the notice date. The caller explains that she received the form but did not know which pay stubs to send because “there was a lot going on at home.” Her son begins mentioning a family illness, then stops, while the information needed for the renewal remains her current income and acceptable proof. Keep the applicable permission requirements in view as you decide what to ask and how to explain the available next steps.
decisions.prompt: What do you ask next?

choices.text: Ask only what the renewal needs: her income and which proof she can get. Say what is fixed and what she can choose, like how to send it.
choices.consequence: You explain the required proof and date, then describe available choices about submission, another copy of the form and reviewing it together. The caller asks which pay stubs count, and you explain the requirements shown for this case without asking about the family situation. She chooses to upload the proof with her son’s help and asks you to remain on the line while she records the date.

feedback.text: Your curiosity had a clear purpose. You asked about the task, not her life, and you kept the real limits visible while giving her real choices inside them. Keep that line: practical help does not depend on sharing a personal history.

Ask the caller to explain the agreed next step in her own words, making clear that you are checking how well you explained it. Use any uncertainty to clarify the information rather than to judge her ability.

choices.text: Ask the caller to tell you more about what was going on at home, so you can note the reason and show the full picture.
choices.consequence: The caller responds, “I’d rather just fix the form,” and her son confirms that she does not want to discuss the family circumstances. The question about acceptable pay stubs remains unanswered, while the conversation has moved beyond the information needed for her stated request.

feedback.text: The renewal needed income and proof, not the story behind the delay. A question like “Which pay stubs are you unsure about?” serves her request. A question about home serves your wish to understand.
To the caller, sharing a hard time with a stranger may feel like the price of getting her coverage back. Her redirect tells you what she wants addressed now. It is not a refusal of help.
When you ask for the reason behind a missed step, who is the question for?

choices.text: Tell the caller you will get the case reopened today, so she does not have to worry about the proof while things are hard at home.
choices.consequence: The caller thanks you, and her son asks, “So we don’t need to send anything now?” making the effect of the promise explicit. Reopening still depends on the required submission and eligibility review, neither of which you can replace with an assurance on this call. The misunderstanding needs correction before the caller relies on the promise and delays sending the form or proof.

feedback.text: Wanting to lift someone’s worry is kind, and it is common under pressure. The readings warn that a promise beyond your authority can undermine trust more than an honest limit. Listening does not create authority to approve a request.

Correct the promise directly: “I cannot reopen coverage myself. The renewal requires these documents by this date, and the person or area responsible reviews them.” Use the current procedure for the actual case.

choices.text: Explain each way she can send proof, such as uploading or mailing it, and the date it is due. Ask whether she has any questions, and when she says no, move on.
choices.consequence: After hearing the submission options and date, the caller initially says she has no questions, but then asks her son which pay stubs count. He is also unsure, showing that the explanation covered delivery methods without resolving the specific information she needed to choose the documents.

feedback.text: You offered real choices, which matters. What was missing was a check on her actual question. “No questions” does not show the explanation worked; an open question about the part that was hard would.
Instead of “Any questions?”, try “Which part would you like me to go over again?” It makes asking easier.

decisions.setup: Before writing the note, you ask the caller to confirm her current communication preference and what was difficult about the notice and the earlier interpreter offer. She explains that the offered interpreter used a language she does not speak and that she could not identify which pay stubs to send. The old note still describes her as unresponsive, and the next worker will rely on the updated record when reviewing further contact. Consider what she has actually confirmed, which arrangements remain unresolved, and where a notice wording concern should be directed.
decisions.prompt: What do you write, and what do you do with what the caller told you?

choices.text: Write what she asked and how she chose to communicate, correct the interpreter record through your unit’s process, and send the pay stub gap to the person or area responsible for notices.
choices.consequence: You record the caller’s question, confirmed communication preference and the submission plan actually agreed during the conversation, without adding a description of her motives. You also record her explanation of the earlier interpreter offer and correct that information through the unit’s established process. The notices team adds the pay-stub wording concern to its review list, without assuming that one account establishes how every caller experiences the letter. Before ending, you explain the next step and check the caller’s understanding, correcting any remaining misunderstanding about submission or eligibility review.

feedback.text: You carried her meaning forward instead of the old inference. The readings show how a note travels: it shapes the next conversation and can become a reason to offer fewer choices. Your note keeps her choices open.

The next worker can see the question the caller asked and the preference she confirmed, instead of relying only on the earlier label. The record supports a better-informed conversation without guaranteeing how that worker will respond.
Keep your claim about the notice honest, as you did: one account names a gap worth checking. It does not prove every notice fails every person.

choices.text: Write a short, helpful note for the next worker: “Caller confused by notice. Son assists. Needs interpreter.” The queue is long, and it covers the main points.
choices.consequence: A later worker reads the new description of confusion and an interpreter need without the caller’s actual language preference or question. In the scenario, an interpreter is again booked in a language she does not use, and she declines the offer. The specific pay-stub concern still has not reached the people responsible for reviewing notices.

feedback.text: “Confused” and “needs interpreter” are new interpretations, not what she said. Compare: “Asked which pay stubs count. Chose English, son on the line.” One records a label; the other records her account.
Which word in your last few notes added a reason the person never gave?
Before saving a note, read it as the next worker would. Ask: will this lead them to ask her, or to assume?

choices.text: Leave the old note as it is and add “Renewal explained.” The call is over, the queue is long, and the old note is not yours to change.
choices.consequence: The record retains the description of an unresponsive client and adds that the renewal was explained, without identifying what the caller asked. A later reviewer would not find her explanation of the interpreter refusal or the unresolved notice wording in that account.

feedback.text: Short notes are a real survival skill on a call line. But the old account still travels. A private change of mind may not repair what the record keeps saying.
To a reviewer months from now, this case reads like a person who would not engage, when in fact she asked a clear question no one had answered.

choices.text: Write an accurate note in plain terms: what she asked, how she chose to communicate and the proof she will send by the date. Leave the notice wording alone; it is not your area.
choices.consequence: The updated note accurately records the caller’s question, communication preference and agreed submission plan for the next worker to consult. However, the notice concern does not reach the person or area responsible, leaving the same wording available to affect another caller.

feedback.text: Your note did right by the caller. The stronger choice also passes her specific point to the person or area responsible, so her knowledge can affect a decision you do not own.
What route do you have for passing a caller’s exact words about a notice to the people who write it?

decisions.setup: The caller has corrected an assumption or become quieter after your opening response, giving you reason to reconsider how the conversation is proceeding. There is still time to ask about her preferences and establish the permissions needed before continuing the discussion of case details.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Name the misstep in one sentence, then ask how she wants to continue: “I assumed instead of asking. How would you like to do the rest of this call?”
choices.consequence: The caller chooses to answer in English with her son present, and you confirm the permission required before discussing case details with him. You explain the continuing offer of a professional interpreter and ask what language she would prefer if she uses that service. She describes the earlier offer in a language she does not speak, allowing that detail to inform the rest of the conversation.

feedback.text: You named the particular assumption without a long apology and without asking her to reassure you. That is what the readings mean by repair: acknowledge the specific inference, then let the person’s answer change what you do.

A concise acknowledgment keeps attention on the caller’s request and gives her room to state a preference. Avoid asking her to reassure you about your intentions while she is seeking help with coverage.

choices.text: Say nothing about the misstep, but slow down, speak more gently and leave longer pauses for the caller to answer for the rest of the call, so she has more room.
choices.consequence: The caller begins answering more often, but nobody explicitly asks how she wants her son involved or confirms the required permission for discussing details. He continues stepping in and mentions the earlier interpreter mismatch in passing, leaving you to verify that account with the caller.

feedback.text: A warmer tone helps, but it is politeness laid over the same pattern. The stronger move asks a question that lets her answer change the call, not just how it sounds.
When you notice a misstep, what makes it hard to say so out loud on a call?

choices.text: Apologize at length, explain that you only meant well and that the queue has you rushing, and ask the caller whether she is okay with you now.
choices.consequence: The caller responds, “It’s fine, it’s fine,” while her son redirects the conversation to the coverage question they called to address. Two minutes have been spent discussing your intention without establishing her communication preferences or the permissions needed for his participation.

feedback.text: Wanting to explain your good intention is a very human reaction to a misstep. The readings point out that defending intention can ask the other person to manage your feelings. Naming the specific mistake does more with less.
Keep a repair to one sentence and one question: what you assumed, and how she would like to continue.

decisions.setup: The caller has declined to discuss personal circumstances, or the available next steps remain unclear despite the explanation you offered. The notice date has not changed, and any promise beyond your authority needs correction before the call ends. Consider how to return to her practical question while stating accurately what you can do and what requires a separate eligibility decision.
decisions.prompt: How do you bring the call back to what she needs?

choices.text: Accept what she has chosen to share, and return to the practical question: “Which part of sending the proof would you like me to explain?”
choices.consequence: The caller asks which pay stubs count, and you explain the requirements and submission options for the fictional case. You clarify that sending the required material allows the renewal to be reviewed, correcting any earlier promise that you could reopen coverage yourself. She chooses the upload option with her son’s help and repeats the notice date before you continue to the case note.

feedback.text: You took her redirect as direction, not resistance. Returning to the practical question kept help available without any cost in disclosure.
What phrase could you keep ready for the moment a caller declines to share something?

choices.text: Explain that knowing why the form was late would help you help her and could go in the note, then ask what was happening at home.
choices.consequence: The caller again declines to describe what happened at home, and her son asks whether another worker can assist with the renewal. You return to the pay-stub question after repeating a request she had already declined, leaving less time to clarify the practical steps.

feedback.text: Making the reason a step toward help turns curiosity into a condition. The stronger choice respects her boundary and still helps.
Her son has requested another worker after the caller declined the personal question twice. Respond to that request under the call-line procedure without assuming either person’s motives.

choices.text: Offer to mail the form again with a list of the proof it needs, and tell her she can call back if anything is still unclear after it arrives.
choices.consequence: You arrange another copy of the form and proof list, but the list still says pay stubs without identifying which ones are needed. The caller thanks you, while the specific document question and whether mailing allows enough time before the deadline remain unresolved.

feedback.text: Sending the form again is a real action, but the same form already confused her. Ask what part is hard before repeating it.
Before you offer a resend, ask: “Would it help to go through it together now?” Let her choose.

practiced: Separating what a person said from the reason a note or a first reading added
Asking how a person wants a call to go instead of guessing from an accent, a name or an old note
Asking only what the task needs, and keeping help available when someone chooses not to share
Explaining what is fixed and what the person can choose, without promising what you cannot decide
Writing a note that carries the person’s own words forward to the next worker
Passing one caller’s account to the person or area responsible without treating it as proof for everyone
this_week: On your next three calls, ask “How would you like to do this call?” before you decide who speaks or in what language.
Open one older note before a call and mark which words describe what happened and which add a reason.
When a caller names a part of a notice that was hard to use, write down their exact words and send them to the person or area responsible.

simulations.intro: If your work involves appeals, HR, legal services, communications or training, you may influence how another person’s account enters the record and is explained. I have seen a documented process leave someone unsure who was hearing their account or what would happen after the conversation. This version follows a DHS fair hearing, asking how you check communication, distinguish testimony from an interpretation and explain the reasons for a recommendation.
simulations.title: The Hearing Record
simulations.learner_role: You are a human services judge in the DHS Appeals Division. You run fair hearings, decide what goes in the record, weigh the evidence and write a recommended decision. You stay impartial between the person appealing and the agency. You control the order of the hearing, the questions you ask and how testimony is described in the decision.
simulations.background: An appellant challenges a reduction in her in-home support hours following a new assessment, with a telephone hearing scheduled for ninety minutes. A phone interpreter, the appellant’s sister and a representative of the county that conducted the assessment have joined the call. You have another hearing afterward, but the schedule does not establish whether communication is working or the necessary evidence has been heard. The case facts and proposed outcome are fictional; actual hearings follow the governing law and current Appeals Division procedures. Related questions about understanding a process and accurately recording an account arise in other enterprise roles, whose authority and procedures differ from a judge’s.

decisions.setup: Before the hearing begins, the appellant asks through the interpreter whether her sister can describe the daily routine she observes. The interpreter reports a connection delay and asks for two repetitions, despite being supplied through the approved vendor arrangement. Your standard opening covers the hearing process using legal terms. Retain the required information while checking how participants can follow it.
decisions.prompt: How do you open the hearing?

choices.text: Read the standard opening script in full, so every required point is covered for the record, and tell the appellant that only parties and witnesses may speak during the hearing.
choices.consequence: After the standard opening, the appellant answers yes when asked whether she understands, but her sister does not offer testimony or seek clarification. Twenty minutes later, the appellant asks why someone from the county is deciding the appeal, revealing that your role remains unclear to her.

feedback.text: Completing the required opening does not establish that participants understood it. Retain the required information, explain your role and the process in plain words, and ask which points need clarification.

From the appellant’s side, she is on a phone call about her care, hearing legal terms through a delayed interpreter, from a person whose role she does not know. “Yes, I understand” may mean “please go on.”

Alongside the required opening, explain that you hear the evidence impartially and prepare a recommendation through the agency’s decision process. Ask what questions remain about your role or what happens next.

choices.text: Check that the appellant can hear the interpreter clearly. In plain words, explain what you decide and the roles people can have. Ask what help she wants from her sister.
choices.consequence: After the interpreter changes connections, you ask participants to confirm that they can hear and explain how to identify any further communication problem. You retain the required opening information and explain your impartial role, the recommendation you prepare and how the final decision is made. The appellant asks to answer herself and have her sister describe the daily routine. You explain how each can take part under the hearing procedure. Both witnesses are sworn, and you state the arrangements on the record. During testimony, continue checking for questions instead of assuming that everyone understands.

feedback.text: You checked the communication arrangement and asked how the appellant wanted her sister involved. Following through under the hearing procedure preserves those choices without treating the vendor arrangement as proof that interpretation is working.

Both parties can refer to the participation arrangements stated on the record. Their clarity supports the hearing process without guaranteeing that the recommendation will withstand any later challenge.

choices.text: Ask the appellant if she agrees, then let her sister answer the questions about the daily routine. She sees it every day, the appellant asked for it, and it will save time.
choices.consequence: The appellant agrees to her sister answering, but begins adding information through the interpreter while her sister is still describing mornings. Their accounts overlap, and the county representative asks whether the appellant will also testify about the assistance she needs. The initial agreement has not settled how to hear both accounts without one replacing or interrupting the other.

feedback.text: The appellant agreed to her sister answering, so the problem is not an absence of consent to that arrangement. Her attempt to add information shows why you also need to clarify how her own account will be heard.

Ask what each person will contribute and explain the participation arrangements under the hearing procedure. A relative’s relevant testimony need not replace the appellant’s opportunity to give her own account.
