choices.text: Apologize warmly and at length for any offense you caused, tell her how much her work matters, and ask whether she can forgive you before you leave today.
choices.consequence: She says it is fine after your extended apology, but you have not identified the factual correction or explained the order’s review route. Her response does not establish why she said it or that the substantive issues are settled. You still need to address the inaccurate account, communication support and applicable review information without making reassurance from her a condition of finishing the visit.

feedback.text: A broad apology that asks for forgiveness puts the work of repair on her. Naming the specific inaccuracy gives her less to manage and more to rely on.
Try: “You kept every entry. I said you did not, and that was not accurate. Here is what the order asks, and here is how you can ask for a review.”

practiced: Going by a person’s stated communication need, and arranging qualified help
Writing what you observed instead of a motive you inferred
Citing what a standard clearly requires, and checking a format question with the person or area responsible
Holding a clear standard while reconsidering your read of the person
Asking about a practice, not about a person’s background
Following an inaccurate word to everywhere it went in the record
Correcting your description of a provider without giving up a real violation
this_week: Reread your last three visit notes. Mark any word that describes a provider’s attitude, and ask what you actually saw.
Check how interpreter requests made at scheduling reach you before a visit, and who to tell when one is missed.
Before your next exit interview, write one sentence that states the violation plainly and one that explains how the provider can ask for a review.
When a provider corrects you this week, try naming the specific thing you got wrong before you explain anything else.

simulations.intro: If you run a program, an implementation plan can describe an arrangement without showing whether people can use it. I have found that the distinction matters when a contract or completed checklist is offered as the evidence of access. Here, you examine a fictional notice requirement, weigh competing uses of a limited budget and report what is known after launch.
simulations.title: Turning a new law into a notice people can use
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Manager. You run a statewide program and supervise three supervisors. You turn legislative requirements into services, decide how staff time and budget are used, and sign off on implementation plans.
simulations.background: In this fictional program, a new law requires a reassessment notice sixty days before each eligibility review, including information about how to request help. Implementation begins in six months, and your plan is due to the division director in three weeks with a fixed amount of new funding. You supervise the call line, notices and policy, and county relations through three supervisors whose evidence needs to inform the plan. The exercise uses an illustrative requirement, so actual notice content, timing and language-access duties must be checked against the law and policy governing your program.

decisions.setup: In the plan review, the notices supervisor walks through the checklist. Next to “People are informed about interpreter services,” the box is checked. The note says, “Interpreter contract in place.” The call-line supervisor frowns. Call-line staff hear from people who did not know they could ask for an interpreter, he says, and some calls end before the person reaches one. The notices supervisor says the contract covers every language the program sees. Both are describing something real.
decisions.prompt: The checklist says met. Your call-line supervisor says people cannot use it. What do you do with that line before you sign the plan?

choices.text: Leave the box checked. The contract covers every language the program sees, which meets the requirement, and the call-line issue is a training question for the call-line team to handle.
choices.consequence: You retain the checked box while asking call-line staff to remind callers about interpreter help, leaving the notice itself without that information. The plan is ready for the deadline, but it still offers the contract as evidence that people know how to request assistance. The call-line supervisor says little afterward; that silence does not establish agreement or explain what he thinks about your decision.

feedback.text: Contracts and checklists feel solid, and deadlines push toward signing. But a contract shows an arrangement, not that people can get the help. The checklist was asking a question the contract does not answer.

Keep the contract information and check the steps people actually use to request help. Set a feasible review date and address known barriers promptly rather than assuming the work always takes one week.

choices.text: Keep the contract details, but mark the line not yet supported. Ask the call-line and notices supervisors how a request works on a real call, and name who checks by when.
choices.consequence: The two supervisors review the notice and authorized call information, finding no interpreter information in the notice and transfers made without an explanation of the wait. The county relations supervisor reports similar questions from counties, adding another source to examine rather than establishing statewide prevalence. You record the evidence gap, identify the people responsible for checking proposed changes and set a review date. The contract remains part of the plan, with practical access still requiring verification.

feedback.text: You kept what is known, the contract, while making the evidence gap visible. That is what a checklist is for: pointing to questions, not settling them. Build on it by asking people who call the line how the help worked for them.

The notices supervisor can contribute contract and wording knowledge while the call-line supervisor brings information about use. Examining those sources together avoids treating either role as a substitute for evidence.
Which checked boxes in your current plans rest on an arrangement, and which rest on evidence that people can use it?

choices.text: Drop the checklist from the plan. If a checked box cannot show whether people actually get help, it is not worth the time, and cutting it frees time for the work that matters.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor removes the checklist, shortening the plan without resolving the call-line concern about interpreter information and transfers. No replacement section identifies who will examine that concern or how the team will check whether callers can reach assistance. Removing a form does not remove the underlying access requirements or the need to demonstrate how they are being met.

feedback.text: You saw the limit of a checked box, which is real. The stronger move keeps the tool and asks for the evidence behind it. A checklist can still point to a useful question.
Next time, ask: “What would show that this line is true for the people calling?” Keep the line open until someone can answer.

choices.text: Act on the call-line concern now. Direct the notices supervisor to translate the notice into ten more languages and add a second interpreter vendor before launch, without waiting for more information.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor begins scoping translation work and another vendor, with estimates that would consume most of the new funding. The call-line supervisor reiterates that the reported problems concern information about help and transfers, which these proposals have not yet addressed. No binding commitment has been made in this exercise, so you can still review the proposed work through the authorized budget and procurement process.

feedback.text: Acting fast on an access concern comes from a good place. But a change made before the concern is examined can miss what people actually face.
A stronger move asks the call-line supervisor what the call notes show first. The evidence may support translation, or something closer to the barrier and less costly.

decisions.setup: Before allocating funds, you check any translation or vendor work proposed earlier and confirm that no binding commitment has reduced the available budget. The approved estimate can fund either peak call-line staffing or a notice rewrite with interpreter information and testing by intended readers; it cannot fully fund both. The notices supervisor favors adding interpreter information while retaining wording she considers consistent, and the call-line supervisor favors additional staff. In this fictional program, legal review has confirmed the required content and sixty-day timing, while allowing the current wording to be revised. Other applicable accessibility, procurement and program requirements still govern either option.
decisions.prompt: Your supervisors disagree, and the money covers one option. How do you make the call?

choices.text: Separate what the law requires from habit. Honor the notices supervisor’s value of consistency, ask whether the same words give people the same chance to act, and say how you will decide.
choices.consequence: You distinguish the required notice content and timing from wording that legal review permits you to change, retaining the other applicable program requirements. The supervisors compare caller questions with the proposal, and the notices supervisor acknowledges that consistent wording may still be difficult for recipients to use. You fund the rewrite and reader testing within the available budget, without also promising the peak staffing option that the same funds cannot cover. You explain the reasons, address the call-transfer problem within existing operations and set a review of testing results and call demand.

feedback.text: You distinguished requirements from revisable wording and chose an option the budget can support. Explain how testing may change the implementation, while retaining applicable access duties and attention to the transfer problem.

Consistency can be a legitimate program aim, but the same words do not demonstrate that every reader can use them. Examine the effect of the wording without assuming that a supervisor’s stated value explains every decision.
Which parts of your program’s routines are required, and which are habits that feel required because they are familiar?

choices.text: Choose the notice rewrite now. The call notes already point clearly to the notice, so there is no need to reopen the debate with the notices supervisor or spend another meeting on it.
choices.consequence: You fund the rewrite but do not clarify how reader testing will be protected within the schedule or how the supervisors will resolve implementation concerns. The notices supervisor later reports omitting the test to meet the deadline, a change that requires your attention regardless of her reasons. Staff prefer the revised wording, but their reaction does not establish whether intended recipients can understand and use it.

feedback.text: The evidence supported examining the notice, but the implementation still needed clear responsibilities and protection for the planned reader test. Address the omitted test rather than treating staff preference as proof of access.
You know the test was omitted and the stated reason was time pressure. Ask about that decision and resolve the implementation problem without attributing an unreported motive to the supervisor.
When the evidence seems to settle a choice, whose reasons do you still need to hear before you decide?

choices.text: Go with the notices supervisor’s view. She leads notices and policy, the notice is her area, and she knows the wording rules better than anyone else at the table.
choices.consequence: You fund peak staffing and retain the notice apart from an interpreter-information line, relying on the notices supervisor’s role without examining the caller evidence together. The additional staff may affect waiting times, but the decision has not addressed whether the existing terms prevent people from understanding the notice. The call-line supervisor’s future willingness to raise concerns is unknown; the present gap is that relevant evidence did not enter the reasoning.

feedback.text: The notices supervisor’s expertise matters, but so does evidence from calls and county partners. Explain how those sources informed the decision instead of relying on organizational role to settle the access question.
Relying on the person whose area it is can feel like good delegation. It works best when that person’s view has been tested against what others know.

choices.text: Split the money evenly between the two options, so neither supervisor feels overruled and both of their concerns get at least some of the new funding this year.
choices.consequence: You divide the funds equally, although the estimates do not support either complete option at that level of funding. The supervisors arrange limited wording edits and some additional staffing, but the planned reader test and full peak coverage cannot proceed as proposed. Those smaller changes may still have effects, yet the split was chosen without evaluating which scoped option would address the documented barriers.

feedback.text: An equal split needs an evidence-based scope and feasible cost, just as choosing one option does. Here the division of funds left both original proposals incomplete without evaluating the smaller alternatives.
Next time, try: “Here is what the law requires. Here is what the evidence shows. Here is my decision and why. Tell me what I might be missing.”

decisions.setup: After the meeting, the call-line supervisor stops by with a printout of call notes. One reads: “Caller asked if someone could explain the letter in her language. Did not know to ask for an interpreter. Transfer dropped.” Another: “Caller’s son interpreted. Unsure of review date.” He says, “This is what the box doesn’t show.”
decisions.prompt: You have the plan in front of you and new information from the call line. What do you do now?

choices.text: Reopen the language-access line. Ask the call-line and notices supervisors to trace one call together, from notice to interpreter, and name who checks the fix by when.
choices.consequence: The supervisors trace an authorized example from notice to interpreter connection and identify missing interpreter information and an unexplained transfer. They also flag a note about a son interpreting as a reason to check whether qualified assistance was offered and understood. The plan identifies proposed corrections, responsible staff and a date to assess the results, with the access claim left unsupported until evidence is available. This example informs the review but does not establish that the same changes will resolve every caller’s barrier or preferences.

feedback.text: You let a concrete account change a plan you had settled. Tracing one real path is often faster than debating the whole system. Next, decide how you will hear from callers after the change.
The call notes changed what the plan needs to verify. Report back on that work without assuming that referral or a revised plan has already resolved the caller’s experience.

choices.text: Thank the call-line supervisor for the notes and add a line to the plan: “Call-line staff report some confusion; monitor after launch.” That records the concern without holding up the deadline.
choices.consequence: The plan now mentions confusion but assigns no one to investigate it and sets no date or method for checking the reported barriers. The note preserves evidence that the concern was raised, while the notice wording and transfer process remain unchanged by your response. What happens after launch is not yet known, and the team has no defined follow-up for finding out.

feedback.text: A note that names a concern without an owner or a date hears it without acting on it. Naming who will check, what, and when turns it into follow-through.
Try asking both supervisors: “Can the two of you own this? What would you need to check it by the end of next month?”

choices.text: Ask the call-line supervisor which caller groups seem most confused, so the plan can target outreach and translated materials to those communities and make the most of a tight budget.
choices.consequence: The call-line supervisor explains that the notes describe individual barriers and do not establish a pattern across a particular community. Your question has not yet produced evidence for selecting groups or addressed the missing information and transfer problem already identified. Targeted outreach may be appropriate when supported by relevant evidence, but these few accounts do not supply that basis.

feedback.text: Wanting to target effort makes sense with a tight budget. But a few individual accounts do not make a group profile. These notes point to a process problem: the notice and the transfer.
When you hear a few accounts, how quickly do you turn them into a statement about a group?

decisions.setup: Four months after launch, the notices supervisor’s draft report equates the absence of formal complaints with a successful notice rollout. The county relations supervisor forwards a county colleague’s report that workers still receive calls from people unsure what the notice requires. That colleague does not know whether other counties see the same problem, and any unresolved notice or transfer issue from earlier decisions still needs attention. Your director asks for an update that distinguishes timely delivery from evidence about whether people can understand and act on the notice.
decisions.prompt: The report says success. A county partner says otherwise. What goes to your director?

choices.text: Report what was done and what is still unknown. Ask the county eligibility supervisor what her workers hear, ask for call-line patterns, and say when she will hear back.
choices.consequence: You report timely notice delivery, no formal complaints and the county’s account of continuing difficulty, without treating any one fact as a complete assessment. You assign a review of authorized call data and reports from three counties, with findings due to the director in six weeks. A focused conversation identifies a potentially confusing sentence about sending forms, which you route for prompt verification and correction without waiting for the broader study. You explain that next step to the county supervisor and commit to an update once the review establishes what changed.

feedback.text: You separated delivery, reported experience and remaining uncertainty, then assigned follow-through. Contact with the county begins that response; an update on the findings and any correction is still needed.

The county supervisor has identified a concern while acknowledging limited knowledge of other counties. Treat both parts of that account as evidence rather than interpreting the qualification as reluctance to complain.
In updates to your director, try three parts: “Here is what was done. Here is what is known about the effect. Here is how and when the agency will learn more.”

choices.text: Send the notices supervisor’s report. No complaints after four months is a good sign, the notice went out on time, and one county’s email is not enough to change the story.
choices.consequence: Your director shares the success claim upward without the county report or a clear distinction between timely delivery and usable instructions. The county supervisor receives no response, and no one is assigned to examine the difficulty her workers reported. Leaders now have an overstated assessment, while the extent and consequences of the possible barrier remain unknown.

feedback.text: An absence of formal complaints does not establish that recipients understood the notice or knew how to challenge a problem. Report the available evidence and its limits while examining the county’s concern.
Compare this with reporting what is known and what is not, and asking the county eligibility supervisor what she sees. One county is not proof of a statewide problem. It is a reason to look.

choices.text: Add the county email to the report as an exception, so the county concern is on record, and keep the overall finding of success that the lack of complaints supports.
choices.consequence: You include the county report but label it an exception before checking whether other counties encounter similar questions. Your director asks county relations to handle it locally, relying on the report’s overall success finding. The county receives thanks, but the program has not examined whether its notice contributes to the concern or whether a broader correction is needed.

feedback.text: Naming the county concern was better than leaving it out. Labeling it an exception decides what it means before anyone checks. A stronger update keeps the effect open and says how you will find out.
When one partner raises a problem, how do you decide whether it is local or a sign of something wider?

choices.text: Ask the county eligibility supervisor to survey her workers and the people they serve, and send you a full analysis before you report anything, so the update rests on real evidence.
choices.consequence: The county eligibility supervisor’s team is already stretched. She replies that she cannot run a survey for a state program. Your update to the director slips. The county’s knowledge reached you, and the request to do the agency’s analysis pushed it back out.

feedback.text: Wanting solid evidence before you report is responsible. But asking a partner to do your team’s analysis shifts staff work onto them.
Ask her one focused question, such as: “What do workers hear most often about the notice?” Then have your own team do the checking.

practiced: Treating a checked box as a question that needs evidence, not as proof of access
Telling an arrangement, like an interpreter contract, apart from whether people can use it
Separating what a law requires from habits that grew around it
Asking whether the same words give people the same chance to act
Weighing front-line and county knowledge alongside policy expertise
Reporting what was done, what is known, and what is still unknown
this_week: Pick one checked line in a current plan. Write down the evidence behind it, and what would show it holds for the people it is meant to reach.
Ask a call-line or county partner one focused question about a notice or process your program runs: what do people find hardest to use?
In your next budget or staffing choice, list what the law requires and what is habit before you compare options.
Look at your most recent status report. Does any line treat “no complaints” as proof that something works?

simulations.intro: If you write policy or guidance, a general statement can become an instruction that shapes many conversations beyond your workgroup. I have learned to check whether background information helps staff ask a useful question or supplies an answer the person never gave. Here, you draft planning guidance, examine a documentation label and report accurately on how workgroup input affected the bulletin.

cast.label: the advocate from a listed community
the advocate who asked for plain language

simulations.title: A bulletin about who is in the room
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Program Consultant. You draft policy bulletins and guidance for county and lead-agency case managers, lead a workgroup of partners, and carry the equity analysis for your drafts. Your words become the instructions case managers follow in thousands of planning meetings.
simulations.background: Your team is writing a bulletin for case managers about support planning meetings for people with disabilities. It tells case managers how to ask whom the person wants at their meeting, and how to document that choice. Person-centered practice and informed choice are at its center. A workgroup reviews your drafts: county and lead-agency staff, two advocates, and a self-advocate who uses services. You send drafts to the workgroup in the format each member asked for, the self-advocate included. Your lead wants the bulletin out before the next planning cycle, six weeks away. The documentation fields live in a statewide system, and changing a field label takes months.

decisions.setup: At the second workgroup meeting, the county lead suggests adding a section called “Cultural considerations.” It would list which communities tend to prefer family-led decisions, so case managers know when to invite family. She has a fact sheet ready. Others nod. It would be quick to add. You notice it would tell case managers what to expect from a person before they ask.
decisions.prompt: The county lead’s idea comes from care and would be easy to add. What do you do with it in the bulletin?

choices.text: Thank the county lead, and use the knowledge to shape questions, not answers. Draft guidance that has case managers ask each person whom they want involved and what would help.
choices.consequence: You use the discussion to develop questions about whom the person wants involved and whether they want any part of the meeting to be private. The county lead helps revise the guidance, which no longer uses community membership to predict an individual’s preference. The self-advocate says the questions better reflect his concern, while the draft still needs review against applicable planning and documentation requirements. That response supports this revision without establishing that he endorses every part of the bulletin.

feedback.text: You kept the county lead’s knowledge and changed its job, from predicting to preparing. At bulletin scale, that choice reaches every planning meeting. Build on it by checking that the documentation guidance records what the person said, not a group expectation.
The county lead contributed to questions that can help case managers prepare. That participation is observable; you do not need to infer her motivation or feelings to recognize the contribution.
Where in your own guidance does background information tell staff what to expect, instead of what to ask?

choices.text: Add the section as the county lead proposed. Case managers keep asking for practical guidance, the fact sheet is well sourced, and it would help them know when to invite family.
choices.consequence: The proposed community list enters the draft as guidance for when to invite family, without a step confirming the individual’s wishes. The self-advocate reads it and stops speaking for the remainder of that discussion, but his silence does not establish agreement or explain his reaction. The current risk is in the instruction itself: group-level information could be used in place of asking the person.

feedback.text: A source can be useful background without establishing an individual preference. Check its relevance and use it to prepare questions, retaining the person’s role and applicable planning requirements.
Compare this with using the same knowledge to write better questions. Case managers still get practical help, and the person still decides.

choices.text: Thank the county lead, but remove all mention of culture and family from the bulletin, so no case manager can read any part of it as stereotyping the people they serve.
choices.consequence: The draft removes references to culture and family without replacing them with practical questions about the person’s preferences or desired support. You have avoided including the proposed list, but have not addressed the workgroup’s concern about how case managers should prepare for those conversations. The county lead’s reaction and the effect on later meetings are not established by removing the section.

feedback.text: Avoiding the subject keeps the bulletin from stereotyping, but it also leaves case managers without a way to ask. Knowledge used to prepare questions is different from knowledge used to predict.
When a topic feels risky, do you tend to cut it or reframe it? What does each cost?

choices.text: Ask the advocate from a listed community, the only workgroup member from one of those communities, to write the section, so it is accurate and draws on lived knowledge.
choices.consequence: The advocate explains that she can contribute experience but cannot describe the preferences of an entire community, and that policy drafting is outside her workgroup role. Your request has not yet produced a suitable section or clarified how her contribution would be used. You remain responsible for drafting guidance that can be reviewed without requiring one participant to represent a population.

feedback.text: To the advocate from a listed community, this asked her to represent a community and do staff work at once. Her knowledge is valuable. It is not a population profile, and the writing is your job.
A stronger path writes guidance that asks each person, then invites her to review a draft if she wants, with clarity about what her review can change.

decisions.setup: After the meeting, the self-advocate sends you a short email. “I keep thinking about the family part. My family matters to me. But some things I want to talk about alone. If the bulletin tells my case manager what people like me want, or tells her nothing at all, she might not ask me.”
decisions.prompt: The self-advocate has named exactly what the guidance could do. What do you do with his email?

choices.text: Reply to the self-advocate with what you will change and when. Rewrite the guidance so it prepares questions and tells case managers to ask the person, and credit his point.
choices.consequence: You explain the revision and when the self-advocate will receive it in the agreed format, then ask how he wants his contribution attributed. The draft directs case managers to ask whom the person wants involved and whether any part of the discussion should be private, within applicable planning requirements. You report the change without sharing his email or identifying him beyond what he has agreed to. If you assigned the other advocate the writing task, you take it back and offer a clearly scoped opportunity to review the staff draft.

feedback.text: You explained the revision and checked attribution rather than assuming permission to share a personal email. Verify that the documentation guidance reflects the same attention to individual preferences.
The self-advocate can review what changed and identify what still concerns him. Neither credit nor an adopted suggestion establishes approval of the entire bulletin.

choices.text: Thank the self-advocate warmly for writing, and tell him his concern will be considered in a later version of the bulletin, once this one is out and case managers have used it.
choices.consequence: You thank him but leave the current draft unchanged and give no defined review date for the concern he has identified. He does not reply before the next meeting, which does not establish whether he agrees, has time to respond or intends to participate again. The draft remains open for revision, so the substantive issue has been deferred rather than resolved.

feedback.text: Being thanked is not the same as being able to influence an open choice. This draft is still open now. A stronger reply says what can change in this version.
When you say “it will be considered,” what does the person hear about what can change?

choices.text: Ask the self-advocate to tell you about his cultural background, so you can understand which groups the guidance affects and make sure the rewrite covers people like him.
choices.consequence: He replies that his concern is about being asked whom he wants involved, not about a group preference linked to his background. Your request for personal history has not answered that point or supplied evidence needed for this revision. You can address the guidance without making further disclosure a condition of examining his concern.

feedback.text: Wanting to understand is a good impulse. Curiosity still needs a purpose tied to the task. The self-advocate’s point does not depend on his background, and making disclosure the price of being heard adds a burden.
Ask about the work instead: “Which part of the section worries you most?”

decisions.setup: The draft now addresses a fictional system field recording who attends a support planning meeting, using two fixed labels: family invited or person declined family involvement. The self-advocate says the second label could misrepresent a wish for privacy during only part of a meeting. Your lead confirms that a label change cannot be delivered this cycle, while approved documentation guidance and a system-change request remain possible. Any unresolved issue from the earlier discussion about asking the person still needs attention.
decisions.prompt: The self-advocate has corrected how the field reads. The labels are fixed for now. What do you do?

choices.text: Name the problem without defending the label. Say what is fixed and what is open, have case managers record the person’s own words in notes, and request a new label.
choices.consequence: You acknowledge the distinction between excluding family entirely and wanting part of a meeting to be private, then revise guidance within the approved documentation process. It directs staff to record relevant preferences accurately in the designated notes field, without adding assumptions about unwillingness or unrelated personal details. You submit a label-change request and explain its review route without promising an implementation date that has not been approved. The self-advocate says the guidance addresses part of the concern, while the fixed label remains a limitation to monitor.

feedback.text: You separated what is fixed from what is open, and used the open part. You also followed the label downstream to the next case manager who will read it. Build on it by checking how case managers use the notes field after release.

The response distinguishes an available guidance change from a pending system request. Keep the workgroup informed of the actual review outcome without guaranteeing how the fixed label will be interpreted.
Which words in your current drafts will be read by someone months from now? What will they assume?

choices.text: Explain to the self-advocate that the label is technically accurate. If he did not want his family invited, he declined, and a careful case manager will read the field neutrally.
choices.consequence: The self-advocate explains that the label does not capture a preference for different participants during different parts of the meeting. You leave the draft without guidance on that distinction, relying on future readers to interpret the field as you do. No later reader’s reaction is known yet, but the documentation problem he identified remains unanswered before release.

feedback.text: A limited field may omit important distinctions even when one selection appears technically available. Use the approved documentation process to preserve relevant preferences and request a better design.
Defending accuracy is natural when you know a system well. A correction is information your first reading missed, not an attack on your work.

choices.text: Tell the self-advocate you will push hard for a better label, and promise him the label will change before the bulletin goes out, so his concern is fixed at the source.
choices.consequence: Your lead confirms again that the system change cannot be delivered before the bulletin, so your promise exceeds the available implementation plan. The draft still lacks guidance for recording preferences accurately under the current labels because you relied on that promised change. You need to correct the assurance and address the available documentation approach before treating the concern as resolved.

feedback.text: Wanting to fix a problem right away is a caring response. But a promise you cannot keep can hurt trust more than an honest limit.
A stronger move says what is fixed and what can change now, then changes what is open. The self-advocate gets real change and an honest timeline.
Explain the current limit, what guidance can change now and when the request will be reviewed. Distinguish a review date from an approved date for a system change.

choices.text: Thank the self-advocate for his perspective and keep the guidance as drafted. The field is out of your control, and the bulletin has to go out before the next planning cycle starts.
choices.consequence: The self-advocate is thanked and nothing changes. The bulletin says nothing about the notes field. You were right that the label was fixed. But the guidance around it was open, and that is where his point could have mattered.

feedback.text: The label was out of your hands. The guidance was not. Listening is valuable, and it is different from letting a concern shape something that is still open.
When part of a decision is fixed, how do you find the part that is still open?

decisions.setup: The draft is approaching release, and your lead proposes marking the equity analysis complete with a general thank-you claiming that the bulletin reflects workgroup input. The record includes suggestions adopted, rejected or still unresolved, depending on the decisions made so far. A requested plain-language version for people using services has no separate funding this cycle, but required access and communication duties still need review before release. No one has checked how case managers will use the guidance, and a funding limit alone does not establish that an access need can wait.
decisions.prompt: How do you close the loop with the workgroup, and with the analysis, before release?

choices.text: Report back plainly: what changed, what did not and why, and who will check how the guidance works after release. Keep the open questions in the equity analysis.
choices.consequence: You describe only the changes actually made, distinguishing them from unresolved guidance, label and access questions left by earlier decisions. You correct any unsupported promise and explain the review of the requested plain-language version, including how required access needs will be met without assuming a future budget approval. You assign an authorized sample review of documentation after release and a report to the workgroup in three months. Relevant findings will be shared without personal case details, while known problems needing action before release remain on the release review.

feedback.text: An accurate account includes adopted suggestions, reasons for other decisions and unresolved requirements. Assign follow-through and report the findings, while addressing release-critical access issues before publication.
The advocate needs a clear explanation of the pending request and its review route. A funding explanation alone does not decide whether an accessible format or communication support is required.
In future report-backs, try three headings: what changed, what did not change and why, and what happens next and when.

choices.text: Send your lead’s thank-you and mark the analysis complete. The workgroup did shape the bulletin, the deadline is close, and a warm note is how most workgroups are closed out.
choices.consequence: The message offers thanks and a broad claim about input without identifying which suggestions changed the draft or which remain unresolved. You mark the analysis complete even though no one has assigned the use review or explained the pending access request. The workgroup’s future participation is unknown; the present record overstates what has been settled.

feedback.text: A thank-you does not show how suggestions informed the draft. Report the actual decisions and open issues, then follow through without promising that a message alone builds trust.
Closing with thanks is common, especially under deadline. It treats acknowledgment as resolution. The harder, more useful step is an honest account.

choices.text: Hold the bulletin until the plain-language version is funded, so everyone’s input is reflected and the advocate who asked for it is not left out of the release.
choices.consequence: Release passes the planned cycle while the separate version remains unfunded, leaving case managers with the earlier guidance. You have not determined how required access needs can be met, which revisions are ready or whether an authorized staged release would address the situation. Delay alone does not settle those questions, just as releasing on schedule would not excuse an unresolved access obligation.

feedback.text: Not wanting to leave anyone’s input behind is a good instinct. But partnership does not mean every request is adopted before anything moves.

Determine which access duties and release conditions apply, then use the authorized decision process. A staged release may be possible, but only if required access and other release conditions are met.

choices.text: Send the thank-you, and add that the bulletin was co-designed with people who use services, so the self-advocate and the advocates get public credit for the work they did.
choices.consequence: The self-advocate writes that reviewing drafts and offering changes did not make him responsible for the whole bulletin or imply agreement with all its choices. The description does not distinguish his contribution from decisions he did not control, including any concern still unresolved in this path. You need to describe the actual process and agree appropriate attribution rather than use participation as an endorsement.

feedback.text: To the self-advocate, “co-designed” turns his feedback into an endorsement of the whole bulletin. Taking part is not approval.
A specific account, naming what his input changed, gives real credit without overstating it.

practiced: Using community knowledge to prepare questions, not to predict a person’s choice
Writing guidance that has staff ask the person whom they want involved
Letting one specific account change a draft, and saying so
Separating what is fixed from what is open, and changing the open part
Following a label or record downstream to the next person who will read it
Reporting back what changed, what did not and why, and when the effect will be checked
this_week: Read one bulletin or guidance draft you own. Find any sentence that tells staff what a group prefers, and rewrite it as a question to ask.
Pick one documentation field or label in your program. Ask how it reads to the next person who opens the record.
Before your next workgroup meeting, write down what is fixed and what is open, and say both at the start.
Draft a report-back for your last round of input: what changed, what did not and why, and what happens next.

simulations.intro: If you supervise a team, your feedback and assignment decisions can affect whose contribution is recognized and who gains experience. I have seen a familiar way of participating become an expectation that no one had actually explained to a new colleague. Here, you review performance evidence, examine a service-plan assumption and respond to a request for accessible updates.

cast.label: the team member who asked for written updates

simulations.title: Feedback, a case review, and a request in a one-to-one
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Supervisor with nine staff. You hold one-to-ones, run team meetings and case reviews, give feedback, and assign work. What you write in feedback and what you notice in meetings shapes who gets the next opportunity.
simulations.background: Your team reviews service plans that county and lead-agency case managers send to DHS. A newer team member joined four months ago from a county job and knows the program well. In meetings she rarely speaks. Afterward she sends careful written comments. A longtime team member said in passing that “people who care speak up in the room.” Mid-year feedback is due Friday. You also run a weekly case review where staff bring hard plans to talk through, and you have one-to-ones on Thursday.

decisions.setup: You are drafting the newer team member’s mid-year feedback. Her written comments caught two errors that changed a plan review. In meetings she has said almost nothing. The longtime team member’s comment is in your head. A sentence sits on your screen: “She should show more engagement by contributing in team discussions.” A stretch assignment, leading reviews of a new plan type, opens next month.
decisions.prompt: What do you write about her participation, and how do you decide?

choices.text: Check the work need and her actual contributions first. In your one-to-one, ask her how she prefers to contribute and what she was told, then write what you observed.
choices.consequence: You recognize the two errors her written comments caught, then ask how she prepares contributions and what expectations were explained when she joined. She describes preferring time to think and says her previous workplace handled unfinished questions differently, without presenting that preference as a community trait. You confirm that her comments arrive before the team’s decisions close and explain the timing needed for future reviews. The feedback describes her work, and you consider her for the stretch assignment against its requirements rather than treating speaking frequency as evidence of commitment.

feedback.text: You checked the work evidence and asked her before deciding what her quiet meant. That kept a familiar style from becoming a judgment about commitment. Build on it by making the team’s expectations clear to the next new hire, too.

Her written comments provide evidence of contribution, while your conversation clarifies how that input can arrive when the team needs it. Ask how she experiences the revised expectations rather than assuming the conversation has secured her trust.
What does engagement look like to you? Where did you learn that, and does the work actually require it?

choices.text: Keep the sentence. Speaking up in meetings is part of the job here, the team decides things out loud, and she will not grow if no one tells her plainly.
choices.consequence: You share the draft before Thursday and name the longtime team member to lead the new plan type without examining the newer colleague’s written contributions. She asks for additional time in her one-to-one after reading the draft, which has not yet been finalized. Both the feedback and the basis for the assignment remain available for review; neither becomes defensible simply because it has been written down.

feedback.text: Many supervisors learned that speaking up shows commitment. It is a common expectation, and it can hide useful knowledge. Speaking is one route to contribution, not the only evidence of it.
Compare this with checking whether her written comments meet the work need. They caught two errors. The question is when the team needs input, not which style is better.
An early judgment can shape assignments and the experience someone gets to build. From her side, this sentence may follow her well past this review.

choices.text: Leave participation out of the feedback so you do not risk being unfair, and give the stretch assignment to the longtime team member, who already leads discussion well.
choices.consequence: The draft omits participation and gives no specific account of the errors her written comments caught or when the team needs input. You give the assignment to the longtime team member based on his visible role in discussions, without comparing relevant work evidence. The newer colleague asks for time in Thursday’s one-to-one, leaving both the incomplete feedback and the assignment rationale open to examination.

feedback.text: Leaving participation out avoided an unsupported sentence but also omitted useful performance evidence. Review the assignment rationale as well as the draft, because an unstated assumption can still affect access to experience.
Who on your team gets stretch work because they are visible? What would it look like to check the work behind the visibility?

choices.text: Write, kindly, that her quietness likely reflects her cultural background, and that the team should be patient with her while she adjusts to a new way of working.
choices.consequence: She reads the draft and asks to discuss the explanation you have attached to her identity, saying it does not describe her reason for writing afterward. The statement has not entered her final review, so you can still correct it and examine whether the same assumption affected another decision. Your intention to be patient does not supply evidence for the explanation you wrote.

feedback.text: An explanation that sounds sympathetic can still assign a meaning the employee never supplied. Ask about her approach and assess the work requirements without treating identity as an explanation of individual behavior.
Describe the work you observed and clarify the expectations that apply. A conversation may help you understand her approach, but it does not guarantee that every issue can be settled at once.
An unsupported statement about identity could mislead later readers of the review. Correct the statement and check whether the same inference affected another personnel decision.

decisions.setup: On Thursday, the newer team member explains that she writes after meetings because she wants to give a complete answer. She asks you to review both the draft feedback and the reasoning behind any assignment decision, including how her written contributions were considered. No one had explained when this team needs input, and the feedback has not yet been finalized.
decisions.prompt: The newer team member has corrected your account. How do you respond?

choices.text: Name the specific thing you got wrong, and thank her for saying it. Ask how the team can get her input in time, and revise the feedback before it is final.
choices.consequence: You identify the inference you made or the contribution you omitted, then revise the draft to describe her work and the timing the team needs. You explain the revision without asking her to reassure you, and agree how written input will reach reviewers before decisions close. You also review whether an unsupported assumption affected the stretch assignment, using the appropriate supervisory process for any resulting correction. That review does not automatically remove the other employee from the assignment, but it prevents a revised sentence from standing in for examination of the decision.

feedback.text: You corrected the written account and examined its possible effect on an assignment. Explain shared expectations to the team, while handling any individual personnel correction through the appropriate process.

Acknowledging the correction without requesting reassurance leaves room for the employee’s account. Continued follow-through, rather than a single conversation, provides evidence of how you respond when feedback challenges your judgment.

choices.text: Explain that you meant well. The feedback was written to help her grow, and you want her to know it came from wanting her to succeed on this team, not from criticism.
choices.consequence: She acknowledges your explanation, but you leave the draft and any assignment rationale unchanged rather than examining the correction she offered. The conversation has therefore added an account of your intention without addressing the evidence behind your earlier description or omission. Her acknowledgment does not establish that she agrees with the draft or considers the matter resolved.

feedback.text: Explaining your intention has not answered the employee’s correction. Revisit the evidence, the draft and any affected decision rather than asking her acknowledgment to stand in for that work.
Try: “I put my own reading on your quiet. That was mine, not what you meant. Here is what I will change.”

choices.text: Apologize warmly for any hurt the draft caused, tell her you value her work, and say the matter is resolved so she does not have to worry about it.
choices.consequence: She thanks you for apologizing, while the draft remains unchanged and the team’s expectations for timely input are still unexplained. You have not reviewed whether the earlier assumption affected an assignment, so that question remains open alongside the written feedback. Declaring the matter resolved goes beyond the changes you have actually made.

feedback.text: The apology acknowledges a concern, but the draft and any affected decision still need examination. Describe what you have actually corrected and what remains to be reviewed.
When someone corrects you, where does your first account go next: a file, an email, an assignment?

decisions.setup: At the weekly review, a county case manager’s plan states that the person receiving services declined an in-home support worker. Its note attributes that decision to a preference among families from the person’s community, without recording an explanation from the person. The presenting reviewer supports that account by referring to something he read about the community, and two colleagues nod. You need to decide how the review will handle an explanation that the available record has not established.
decisions.prompt: The presenting reviewer has used a general statement about a community to explain one person’s choice. How do you respond in the case review?

choices.text: Thank the presenting reviewer for raising it, then ask what the person actually said and what the note added. Suggest the review ask the case manager what the person wants.
choices.consequence: You ask the reviewers to distinguish the recorded decision from the reason attributed to it, and the presenting reviewer acknowledges that the reason is unknown. The second reviewer offers several possible explanations, which the team treats as questions rather than substitute conclusions about this person. The review asks the case manager to clarify the person’s own preferences and whom they want involved, using the applicable planning process. The presenting reviewer says he intends to use that distinction in future reviews, although the requested clarification is still needed in this case.

feedback.text: You noticed a moment where identity came up and used it for learning, not blame. Separating what the person said from what was added is the core move. Build on it by bringing that question to every case review, not only when a community is named.

The reviewer acknowledged the gap after you asked about the evidence. A question can make that distinction clear, but it does not guarantee comfort or remove the need to correct an unsupported record.
In your own reviews, how often does a note explain a choice the person never explained?

choices.text: Let it pass. The presenting reviewer is drawing on real knowledge of the community, the case manager knows the family, and the plan otherwise looks complete and ready to approve.
choices.consequence: The review approves the plan without asking the case manager to clarify the person’s explanation or preferences through the applicable planning process. The community-based claim remains in the record, where a later reader could mistake it for information supplied by the person. No future service decision is established here; the current problem is that an unsupported explanation has been allowed to travel with the plan.

feedback.text: Knowledge about a community can suggest useful questions, but it does not establish why an individual declined a particular service. The review needs information from the person through the appropriate planning process.

Ask what the person said and what the note added, then follow through on the clarification. The time required will vary; a brief question alone does not correct a record or establish the person’s wishes.

choices.text: Tell the presenting reviewer plainly, in front of the team, that his comment is a stereotype about a community, so everyone hears that it is not acceptable, and move to the next case.
choices.consequence: You identify the stereotype and move to the next case, sending the plan back with instructions to remove the unsupported community claim. The review does not ask what the person wanted or why the particular support was declined, so the relevant planning question remains unanswered. Removing the claim addresses part of the record, but does not supply the information needed to understand this person’s decision.

feedback.text: Naming a stereotype can be appropriate. The missing step is examining the evidence and obtaining the person’s preferences before treating the planning question as settled.

A supervisor can address an unsupported generalization clearly while keeping attention on the person and the record. Neither a firm correction nor a gentle question guarantees how colleagues will respond.
The team has heard that the generalization is unacceptable, but has not practiced how to replace it with relevant evidence. Continue the review rather than leaving the lesson at removal of a phrase.

choices.text: Ask the second reviewer, who shares a background with the family, whether the presenting reviewer is right, so the team hears from someone with direct knowledge before the plan is approved.
choices.consequence: The second reviewer says she can describe her own experience but cannot explain this person’s decision or represent an entire community. Her response does not confirm the note, and the team still lacks an account of the person’s preferences. Asking her because of a shared background has added a burden without resolving the question the case manager needs to clarify.

feedback.text: To the second reviewer, this turns her identity into a team resource. No one should be asked to represent an entire community, least of all in front of peers.
Use the case manager’s planning process to ask what the person wants and whom they want involved. A shared background does not authorize a colleague to answer for them.
Who on your team gets asked to explain a group? How often did they agree to that role?

decisions.setup: In a Thursday one-to-one, a team member says the morning huddle is hard for her. The room is loud, and with her hearing loss she misses parts of the spoken updates. She asks whether she could get the updates in writing. She has not used the word accommodation. The longtime team member runs the huddle and likes it short and spoken.
decisions.prompt: She has asked for written updates and connected it to her hearing. What do you do?

choices.text: Treat it as a request tied to her hearing. Forward it today, tell her who decides, do not ask about her diagnosis, and start written huddle notes for everyone.
choices.consequence: You forward the request that afternoon and identify the decision maker, while leaving medical-documentation questions to the ADA Coordinator. In a private conversation, you ask which updates she misses and whether written notes would address that practical barrier. You begin notes as a routine within your authority without sharing the reason for her request with colleagues. You check whether they help her participate, while the formal process continues; notes helping other staff does not establish that her access need has been met.

feedback.text: You recognized the request, protected its privacy and forwarded it promptly. A practical adjustment can proceed within your authority while the accommodation process determines what is effective.

Identifying the decision maker explains the next step; it does not give the employee sole control over the outcome. Ask about the work barrier without seeking medical details, and keep her informed as the process continues.
Which of your team routines could change today, and which need another person to decide?

choices.text: Ask her about her diagnosis and whether she has documentation from a doctor, so you can make a fair decision and treat her request the same way as anyone else’s.
choices.consequence: She pauses and says she will think about your question, while you have not yet forwarded the request or arranged written updates. Her response does not withdraw the request or show that the barrier has disappeared, so the obligation to process it remains. You need to correct your handling rather than wait for her to repeat the request or bring medical material to you.

feedback.text: Wanting to be fair is reasonable. The readings are plain on this point: supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation from the person seeking an accommodation, and appropriate requests belong to the agency ADA Coordinator. A stronger move forwards the request promptly and tells her who decides.
Your medical question introduced a demand outside your supervisory role in this process. Correct it and forward the request; do not treat her hesitation as a withdrawal.

choices.text: Bring it to the team meeting. Say someone asked for written updates because of trouble hearing in the huddle, and ask everyone whether they prefer a spoken or a written huddle.
choices.consequence: You describe a hearing-related request to colleagues who do not need that information, then invite a vote on the huddle format. The team chooses to keep spoken updates, but that preference does not decide the accommodation request or remove the need to forward it. You must address the disclosure through the appropriate agency process while promptly routing the still-unresolved request.

feedback.text: A team conversation about formats can be useful, but not as the way to decide one person’s request. Her request goes to the decision maker. A vote is not that process.

The request should be handled with people who need the information to process or implement it. Omitting a name does not necessarily protect privacy when colleagues can infer whose situation is being discussed.
Next time, try: “I will forward this today to the person who decides, and tell you who that is. Separately, I can send huddle notes to everyone.”

choices.text: Tell her you will ask the longtime team member to speak louder and slow down in huddles, and see if that helps over the next few weeks before you forward anything.
choices.consequence: The huddle leader speaks louder for several days, but you have not checked whether that change addresses the employee’s access barrier. You also have not forwarded her request, leaving the decision maker unable to act on the information she supplied to you. The request still needs prompt processing rather than waiting several weeks to see whether your proposed adjustment is sufficient.

feedback.text: Trying a quick fix yourself is a common and caring response. But a request connected to a medical condition needs to reach the decision maker promptly. Your fix and the formal process can both happen.
Compare this with forwarding the request today and also changing what you control. She gets both the quick help and the formal route.

practiced: Checking the work evidence before deciding what a quiet colleague’s style means
Writing feedback that describes what you observed, not a label
Naming the specific inference when someone corrects you, and fixing the record
Separating what a person said from what a note or a general statement added
Using a case review moment for learning without shaming or asking one person to speak for a group
Forwarding a request promptly without asking for medical details, while changing what you control
this_week: Reread one piece of feedback you have written this year. Mark any word that describes a motive rather than what you saw.
Tell your team, in one or two sentences, how and when you want input before decisions close, including in writing.
In your next case review, ask once: “What did the person say, and what did the note add?”
Find out who decides accommodation requests for your team, so you can name that person right away when someone asks.

action_plan: Choose one label you tend to use at work, such as quiet, reluctant or not interested, and practice rewriting it as what you actually observed.
Before your next question to someone you serve or work with, ask yourself what you will do with the answer.
When you invite input, say what is already decided, what is open and how the input can change the next step.
The next time someone corrects you, name the specific thing you got wrong, then check where your first account traveled.
Pick one checklist or tool you use and identify one answer that needs evidence from the people affected.
When you report on a change, keep apart what you learned, what you did and what is still unknown about its effect.

closing.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Keep the next question open. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands loosely clasped, as at the opening.
on_screen: Knowledge informs the question.
The person holds the answer about their own life.
Keep the next question open.
closing.narration: The course began with an appointment letter that gave the correct address while leaving a visitor unable to identify the public entrance. That example shows why professional knowledge and a person's experience need to inform the same decision, even when they answer different questions. Cultural humility involves examining the meaning you add, asking with a useful purpose and considering how your role shapes the response. It also involves allowing another person's account to influence a choice and repairing an interpretation that has caused difficulty or traveled into a record. None of these practices establishes mastery of someone else's culture, and each leaves room for another question or correction. Return to the situation you considered at the beginning and identify what you would now want to understand more clearly. A specific question and a response within your responsibility provide a practical place to continue the work.

facilitator.purpose: Help colleagues practice ongoing self-examination, attention to unequal influence and partnership while considering the responsibilities that apply in their DHS roles. Use the simulation to examine interpretations, compare possible responses and identify one concrete practice that participants can apply in their work. Keep discussion focused on the fictional examples so no one needs to disclose personal experiences or represent a community.
delivery: Individually: each person watches the segments and works through the simulation, then brings one reflection to a team conversation.
As a team session of about 90 minutes: watch segments together, pause for the checks, and run the simulation as a group, voting on each choice.
As two shorter sessions: segments one to three in the first, segments four to six and the simulation in the second, one to two weeks apart.
Works in person or online. Online, use a poll for simulation choices and invite chat responses for people who prefer to write first.
preparation: Watch all six segments and play the simulation at least twice, once choosing strong options and once choosing weaker ones, so you know the recovery paths.
Read the reflection questions and pick two per segment that fit your group.
Think of a small, low-stakes example from your own work where you added a meaning someone had not given. You may share it to set the tone.
Share the agenda and the simulation premise with participants a day ahead, so people who like to think first can do so.

Check current DHS contacts and procedures for Human Resources, Equal Opportunity and Access, and accommodations. Employees are expected to report complaints promptly; supervisors must also follow Policy 1436 and DHS referral procedures.

agenda.title: Opening and why it matters
steps: Welcome the group and name one thing you are curious to learn from them today.
Play segment one, Welcome and why it matters.
Ask the group the entrance check question and take two or three answers.
notes: Keep the discussion focused on the information available to each person. Ask what the checked address establishes and what the visitor’s account still leaves unresolved.

agenda.title: What it is and your own assumptions
steps: Run the observation versus inference exercise: offer quiet in the meeting, declined help and questioned the instruction, and ask pairs to write what was observed and one question that could change the reading.
Take a few examples back to the full group.
notes: Use the practice phrases rather than real cases about named people.

agenda.title: Practices and recovery
steps: Ask: which of the three sideways repairs, defending, seeking reassurance or declaring it fixed, is most familiar?
Have pairs practice one correction line out loud, naming a specific inference.
notes: If a concern surfaces, move personal details out of the group discussion and explain the reporting responsibilities that apply. DHS expects employees to report discrimination, harassment or retaliation complaints promptly. Managers and supervisors report protected-class allegations immediately under Policy 1436 and follow DHS referral procedures without waiting for proof or for the session to end.

agenda.title: Bringing it into the work
steps: Ask each person to name one checklist, form or routine in their work that could do more with input from the people affected.

agenda.title: Simulation: The visitor letter
steps: Run the simulation as a group. Read each setup aloud. Ask everyone to pick a choice silently, then hear two or three reasons. Pick the group's choice by a show of hands and play its consequence and coaching.
Try at least one weaker choice on purpose to show a recovery decision.
After the last decision, read the practiced list aloud.
notes: Ask the group whose view they found hardest to see: the visitor, the experienced teammate, the newer teammate or the team lead.

agenda.title: Closing and commitments
steps: Ask each person to pick one action plan item to try this week, privately or out loud.

say: Your knowledge of the work helps you ask useful questions, but it may not explain how another person experiences the same process.
Consider a letter that gives the correct address while leaving a visitor unable to identify the public entrance. What additional information would help someone review that problem?
The readings connect cultural humility with examining your assumptions, attending to differences in influence, and developing partnerships that give people meaningful choices.
Professional expertise remains useful when you distinguish what it establishes from what you still need to learn through the person’s account.
The form was not returned is an observation; the person is not interested adds an explanation that the observation alone does not establish. What question could help examine that explanation?
When an explanation comes to mind quickly, pause to distinguish the evidence you have from the meaning you have added to it.

When someone corrects an interpretation, consider naming the specific inference you got wrong before explaining what you intended. This keeps attention on the correction rather than asking the person to reassure you.
For example: “I assumed your concern was about the topic, but you were asking about the deadline. Thank you for clarifying that.”
First decision: what did the visitor actually say, and what question does the address answer?
Thread decision: what does the team actually need before Friday, and does written input meet it?
Closing the loop: what did the team change, what belongs to someone else, and how would anyone know it works?

The address was accurate, written input arrived before the deadline, and the visitor described a real difficulty finding the entrance. Which response used those facts, and which response treated one fact as if it answered every question?
Which moment in the simulation felt most like your real job?
Cultural humility continues as you encounter new information, responsibilities and interpretations in your work; completing a course does not settle that practice.
Choose one action to try this week, then examine what happened and what remains uncertain before deciding on a further step.

when_stalls: Share your own small example first: a time you added a reason someone had not given, and what you learned.
Ask people to write for one minute before anyone speaks, then invite a few to read what they wrote.
Switch to pairs for two minutes, then ask each pair for one sentence.
Ask a concrete question: Where in your work does a correct answer sometimes stand in for a usable one?
when_tense: If someone feels blamed: “This is about the work, not anyone's worth. What does the process assume, and what did a person tell you it missed?”
If someone says humility means giving people whatever they want: “It does not. You can understand a request, explain a real limit and still look for an option.”
If a person is asked to speak for a group: “Nobody here speaks for a whole community. Speak from your own experience if you choose to.”
Thank the person and move personal details out of the group. Explain employee reporting expectations and supervisors’ immediate duties under Policy 1436.
Follow the current DHS referral procedure without asking for proof or promising secrecy. A supervisor’s required report must not wait until the session ends.
follow_up: Two weeks later, ask the team which action plan item they tried and what they noticed.
Invite the team to pick one shared routine, such as an agenda, a letter or a tracker, and look at it together with the question: what does this assume people already know?
Encourage teams to build simple feedback loops so they hear how the people they serve actually experience their work.
Point people to the readings listed at the end of the course, including the Hook, Davis, Owen and DeBlaere book and the Tervalon and Murray-García paper.

version_notes.enterprise-services: If your work is HR, communications, legal or training, the same three moments come up in an interview, a public message or a course: who understands the process, how someone’s account is written down, and what the final document says about them.
